sections.title: Competence
sections.text:
§ 10.35 Competence.
(a) A practitioner must possess the necessary competence to engage in practice before the Internal Revenue Service. Competent practice requires the appropriate level of knowledge, skill, thoroughness, and preparation necessary for the matter for which the practitioner is engaged. A practitioner may become competent for the matter for which the practitioner has been engaged through various methods, such as consulting with experts in the relevant area or studying the relevant law.
(b) Effective/applicability date. This section is applicable beginning June 12, 2014.
[T.D. 9668, 79 FR 33693, June 12, 2014]

parts.title: 31 CFR Part 10 Subparts A & C — Renewal, Continuing Education & Sanctions

sections.title: Term and renewal of status as an enrolled agent, enrolled retirement plan agent, or registered tax return preparer
sections.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 31 CFR § 10.6 — Term and renewal of enrolled agent status
sections.officialGuideLabel: IRS.gov — Become an Enrolled Agent & Renewal Rules
sections.text:
§ 10.6 Term and renewal of status as an enrolled agent, enrolled retirement plan agent, or registered tax return preparer.
(a) Term. Each individual authorized to practice before the Internal Revenue Service as an enrolled agent, enrolled retirement plan agent, or registered tax return preparer will be accorded active enrollment or registration status subject to renewal of enrollment or registration as provided in this part.
(b) Enrollment or registration card or certificate. The Internal Revenue Service will issue an enrollment or registration card or certificate to each individual whose application to practice before the Internal Revenue Service is approved. Each card or certificate will be valid for the period stated on the card or certificate. An enrolled agent, enrolled retirement plan agent, or registered tax return preparer may not practice before the Internal Revenue Service if the card or certificate is not current or otherwise valid. The card or certificate is in addition to any notification that may be provided to each individual who obtains a preparer tax identification number.
(c) Change of address. An enrolled agent, enrolled retirement plan agent, or registered tax return preparer must send notification of any change of address to the address specified by the Internal Revenue Service within 60 days of the change of address. This notification must include the enrolled agent's, enrolled retirement plan agent's, or registered tax return preparer's name, prior address, new address, tax identification number(s) (including preparer tax identification number), and the date the change of address is effective. Unless this notification is sent, the address for purposes of any correspondence from the appropriate Internal Revenue Service office responsible for administering this part shall be the address reflected on the practitioner's most recent application for enrollment or registration, or application for renewal of enrollment or registration. A practitioner's change of address notification under this part will not constitute a change of the practitioner's last known address for purposes of section 6212 of the Internal Revenue Code and regulations thereunder.
(d) Renewal—(1) In general. Enrolled agents, enrolled retirement plan agents, and registered tax return preparers must renew their status with the Internal Revenue Service to maintain eligibility to practice before the Internal Revenue Service. Failure to receive notification from the Internal Revenue Service of the renewal requirement will not be justification for the individual's failure to satisfy this requirement.
(2) Renewal period for enrolled agents. (i) All enrolled agents must renew their preparer tax identification number as prescribed by forms, instructions, or other appropriate guidance.
(ii) Enrolled agents who have a Social Security number or tax identification number that ends with the numbers 0, 1, 2, or 3, except for those individuals who received their initial enrollment after November 1, 2003, must apply for renewal between November 1, 2003, and January 31, 2004. The renewal will be effective April 1, 2004.
(iii) Enrolled agents who have a social security number or tax identification number that ends with the numbers 4, 5, or 6, except for those individuals who received their initial enrollment after November 1, 2004, must apply for renewal between November 1, 2004, and January 31, 2005. The renewal will be effective April 1, 2005.
(iv) Enrolled agents who have a social security number or tax identification number that ends with the numbers 7, 8, or 9, except for those individuals who received their initial enrollment after November 1, 2005, must apply for renewal between November 1, 2005, and January 31, 2006. The renewal will be effective April 1, 2006.
(v) Thereafter, applications for renewal as an enrolled agent will be required between November 1 and January 31 of every subsequent third year as specified in paragraph (d)(2)(i), (d)(2)(ii), or (d)(2)(iii) of this section according to the last number of the individual's Social Security number or tax identification number. Those individuals who receive initial enrollment as an enrolled agent after November 1 and before April 2 of the applicable renewal period will not be required to renew their enrollment before the first full renewal period following the receipt of their initial enrollment.
(3) Renewal period for enrolled retirement plan agents. (i) All enrolled retirement plan agents must renew their preparer tax identification number as prescribed by the Internal Revenue Service in forms, instructions, or other appropriate guidance.
(ii) Enrolled retirement plan agents will be required to renew their status as enrolled retirement plan agents between April 1 and June 30 of every third year subsequent to their initial enrollment.
(4) Renewal period for registered tax return preparers. Registered tax return preparers must renew their preparer tax identification number and their status as a registered tax return preparer as prescribed by the Internal Revenue Service in forms, instructions, or other appropriate guidance.
(5) Notification of renewal. After review and approval, the Internal Revenue Service will notify the individual of the renewal and will issue the individual a card or certificate evidencing current status as an enrolled agent, enrolled retirement plan agent, or registered tax return preparer.
(6) Fee. A reasonable nonrefundable fee may be charged for each application for renewal filed. See 26 CFR part 300.
(7) Forms. Forms required for renewal may be obtained by sending a written request to the address specified by the Internal Revenue Service or from such other source as the Internal Revenue Service will publish in the Internal Revenue Bulletin (see 26 CFR 601.601(d)(2)(ii)(b)) and on the Internal Revenue Service webpage (http://www.irs.gov).
(e) Condition for renewal: continuing education. In order to qualify for renewal as an enrolled agent, enrolled retirement plan agent, or registered tax return preparer, an individual must certify, in the manner prescribed by the Internal Revenue Service, that the individual has satisfied the requisite number of continuing education hours.
(1) Definitions. For purposes of this section—
(i) Enrollment year means January 1 to December 31 of each year of an enrollment cycle.
(ii) Enrollment cycle means the three successive enrollment years preceding the effective date of renewal.
(iii) Registration year means each 12-month period the registered tax return preparer is authorized to practice before the Internal Revenue Service.
(iv) The effective date of renewal is the first day of the fourth month following the close of the period for renewal described in paragraph (d) of this section.
(2) For renewed enrollment as an enrolled agent or enrolled retirement plan agent—(i) Requirements for enrollment cycle. A minimum of 72 hours of continuing education credit, including six hours of ethics or professional conduct, must be completed during each enrollment cycle.
(ii) Requirements for enrollment year. A minimum of 16 hours of continuing education credit, including two hours of ethics or professional conduct, must be completed during each enrollment year of an enrollment cycle.
(iii) Enrollment during enrollment cycle—(A) In general. Subject to paragraph (e)(2)(iii)(B) of this section, an individual who receives initial enrollment during an enrollment cycle must complete two hours of qualifying continuing education credit for each month enrolled during the enrollment cycle. Enrollment for any part of a month is considered enrollment for the entire month.
(B) Ethics. An individual who receives initial enrollment during an enrollment cycle must complete two hours of ethics or professional conduct for each enrollment year during the enrollment cycle. Enrollment for any part of an enrollment year is considered enrollment for the entire year.
(3) Requirements for renewal as a registered tax return preparer. A minimum of 15 hours of continuing education credit, including two hours of ethics or professional conduct, three hours of Federal tax law updates, and 10 hours of Federal tax law topics, must be completed during each registration year.
(f) Qualifying continuing education—(1) General—(i) Enrolled agents. To qualify for continuing education credit for an enrolled agent, a course of learning must—
(A) Be a qualifying continuing education program designed to enhance professional knowledge in Federal taxation or Federal tax related matters (programs comprised of current subject matter in Federal taxation or Federal tax related matters, including accounting, tax return preparation software, taxation, or ethics); and
(B) Be a qualifying continuing education program consistent with the Internal Revenue Code and effective tax administration.
(ii) Enrolled retirement plan agents. To qualify for continuing education credit for an enrolled retirement plan agent, a course of learning must—
(A) Be a qualifying continuing education program designed to enhance professional knowledge in qualified retirement plan matters; and
(B) Be a qualifying continuing education program consistent with the Internal Revenue Code and effective tax administration.
(iii) Registered tax return preparers. To qualify for continuing education credit for a registered tax return preparer, a course of learning must—
(A) Be a qualifying continuing education program designed to enhance professional knowledge in Federal taxation or Federal tax related matters (programs comprised of current subject matter in Federal taxation or Federal tax related matters, including accounting, tax return preparation software, taxation, or ethics); and
(B) Be a qualifying continuing education program consistent with the Internal Revenue Code and effective tax administration.
(2) Qualifying programs—(i) Formal programs. A formal program qualifies as a continuing education program if it—
(A) Requires attendance and provides each attendee with a certificate of attendance;
(B) Is conducted by a qualified instructor, discussion leader, or speaker (in other words, a person whose background, training, education, and experience is appropriate for instructing or leading a discussion on the subject matter of the particular program);
(C) Provides or requires a written outline, textbook, or suitable electronic educational materials; and
(D) Satisfies the requirements established for a qualified continuing education program pursuant to § 10.9.
(ii) Correspondence or individual study programs (including taped programs). Qualifying continuing education programs include correspondence or individual study programs that are conducted by continuing education providers and completed on an individual basis by the enrolled individual. The allowable credit hours for such programs will be measured on a basis comparable to the measurement of a seminar or course for credit in an accredited educational institution. Such programs qualify as continuing education programs only if they—
(A) Require registration of the participants by the continuing education provider;
(B) Provide a means for measuring successful completion by the participants (for example, a written examination), including the issuance of a certificate of completion by the continuing education provider;
(C) Provide a written outline, textbook, or suitable electronic educational materials; and
(D) Satisfy the requirements established for a qualified continuing education program pursuant to § 10.9.
(iii) Serving as an instructor, discussion leader or speaker. (A) One hour of continuing education credit will be awarded for each contact hour completed as an instructor, discussion leader, or speaker at an educational program that meets the continuing education requirements of paragraph (f) of this section.
(B) A maximum of two hours of continuing education credit will be awarded for actual subject preparation time for each contact hour completed as an instructor, discussion leader, or speaker at such programs. It is the responsibility of the individual claiming such credit to maintain records to verify preparation time.
(C) The maximum continuing education credit for instruction and preparation may not exceed four hours annually for registered tax return preparers and six hours annually for enrolled agents and enrolled retirement plan agents.
(D) An instructor, discussion leader, or speaker who makes more than one presentation on the same subject matter during an enrollment cycle or registration year will receive continuing education credit for only one such presentation for the enrollment cycle or registration year.
(3) Periodic examination. Enrolled Agents and Enrolled Retirement Plan Agents may establish eligibility for renewal of enrollment for any enrollment cycle by—
(i) Achieving a passing score on each part of the Special Enrollment Examination administered under this part during the three year period prior to renewal; and
(ii) Completing a minimum of 16 hours of qualifying continuing education during the last year of an enrollment cycle.
(g) Measurement of continuing education coursework. (1) All continuing education programs will be measured in terms of contact hours. The shortest recognized program will be one contact hour.
(2) A contact hour is 50 minutes of continuous participation in a program. Credit is granted only for a full contact hour, which is 50 minutes or multiples thereof. For example, a program lasting more than 50 minutes but less than 100 minutes will count as only one contact hour.
(3) Individual segments at continuous conferences, conventions and the like will be considered one total program. For example, two 90-minute segments (180 minutes) at a continuous conference will count as three contact hours.
(4) For university or college courses, each semester hour credit will equal 15 contact hours and a quarter hour credit will equal 10 contact hours.
(h) Recordkeeping requirements. (1) Each individual applying for renewal must retain for a period of four years following the date of renewal the information required with regard to qualifying continuing education credit hours. Such information includes—
(i) The name of the sponsoring organization;
(ii) The location of the program;
(iii) The title of the program, qualified program number, and description of its content;
(iv) Written outlines, course syllibi, textbook, and/or electronic materials provided or required for the course;
(v) The dates attended;
(vi) The credit hours claimed;
(vii) The name(s) of the instructor(s), discussion leader(s), or speaker(s), if appropriate; and
(viii) The certificate of completion and/or signed statement of the hours of attendance obtained from the continuing education provider.
(2) To receive continuing education credit for service completed as an instructor, discussion leader, or speaker, the following information must be maintained for a period of four years following the date of renewal—
(i) The name of the sponsoring organization;
(ii) The location of the program;
(iii) The title of the program and copy of its content;
(iv) The dates of the program; and
(v) The credit hours claimed.
(i) Waivers. (1) Waiver from the continuing education requirements for a given period may be granted for the following reasons—
(i) Health, which prevented compliance with the continuing education requirements;
(ii) Extended active military duty;
(iii) Absence from the United States for an extended period of time due to employment or other reasons, provided the individual does not practice before the Internal Revenue Service during such absence; and
(iv) Other compelling reasons, which will be considered on a case-by-case basis.
(2) A request for waiver must be accompanied by appropriate documentation. The individual is required to furnish any additional documentation or explanation deemed necessary. Examples of appropriate documentation could be a medical certificate or military orders.
(3) A request for waiver must be filed no later than the last day of the renewal application period.
(4) If a request for waiver is not approved, the individual will be placed in inactive status. The individual will be notified that the waiver was not approved and that the individual has been placed on a roster of inactive enrolled agents, enrolled retirement plan agents, or registered tax return preparers.
(5) If the request for waiver is not approved, the individual may file a protest as prescribed by the Internal Revenue Service in forms, instructions, or other appropriate guidance. A protest filed under this section is not governed by subpart D of this part.
(6) If a request for waiver is approved, the individual will be notified and issued a card or certificate evidencing renewal.
(7) Those who are granted waivers are required to file timely applications for renewal of enrollment or registration.
(j) Failure to comply. (1) Compliance by an individual with the requirements of this part is determined by the Internal Revenue Service. The Internal Revenue Service will provide notice to any individual who fails to meet the continuing education and fee requirements of eligibility for renewal. The notice will state the basis for the determination of noncompliance and will provide the individual an opportunity to furnish the requested information in writing relating to the matter within 60 days of the date of the notice. Such information will be considered in making a final determination as to eligibility for renewal. The individual must be informed of the reason(s) for any denial of a renewal. The individual may, within 30 days after receipt of the notice of denial of renewal, file a written protest of the denial as prescribed by the Internal Revenue Service in forms, instructions, or other appropriate guidance. A protest under this section is not governed by subpart D of this part.
(2) The continuing education records of an enrolled agent, enrolled retirement plan agent, or registered tax return preparer may be reviewed to determine compliance with the requirements and standards for renewal as provided in paragraph (f) of this section. As part of this review, the enrolled agent, enrolled retirement plan agent or registered tax return preparer may be required to provide the Internal Revenue Service with copies of any continuing education records required to be maintained under this part. If the enrolled agent, enrolled retirement plan agent or registered tax return preparer fails to comply with this requirement, any continuing education hours claimed may be disallowed.
(3) An individual who has not filed a timely application for renewal, who has not made a timely response to the notice of noncompliance with the renewal requirements, or who has not satisfied the requirements of eligibility for renewal will be placed on a roster of inactive enrolled individuals or inactive registered individuals. During this time, the individual will be ineligible to practice before the Internal Revenue Service.
(4) Individuals placed in inactive status and individuals ineligible to practice before the Internal Revenue Service may not state or imply that they are eligible to practice before the Internal Revenue Service, or use the terms enrolled agent, enrolled retirement plan agent, or registered tax return preparer, the designations “EA” or “ERPA” or other form of reference to eligibility to practice before the Internal Revenue Service.
(5) An individual placed in inactive status may be reinstated to an active status by filing an application for renewal and providing evidence of the completion of all required continuing education hours for the enrollment cycle or registration year. Continuing education credit under this paragraph (j)(5) may not be used to satisfy the requirements of the enrollment cycle or registration year in which the individual has been placed back on the active roster.
(6) An individual placed in inactive status must file an application for renewal and satisfy the requirements for renewal as set forth in this section within three years of being placed in inactive status. Otherwise, the name of such individual will be removed from the inactive status roster and the individual's status as an enrolled agent, enrolled retirement plan agent, or registered tax return preparer will terminate. Future eligibility for active status must then be reestablished by the individual as provided in this section.
(7) Inactive status is not available to an individual who is the subject of a pending disciplinary matter before the Internal Revenue Service.
(k) Inactive retirement status. An individual who no longer practices before the Internal Revenue Service may request to be placed in an inactive retirement status at any time and such individual will be placed in an inactive retirement status. The individual will be ineligible to practice before the Internal Revenue Service. An individual who is placed in an inactive retirement status may be reinstated to an active status by filing an application for renewal and providing evidence of the completion of the required continuing education hours for the enrollment cycle or registration year. Inactive retirement status is not available to an individual who is ineligible to practice before the Internal Revenue Service or an individual who is the subject of a pending disciplinary matter under this part.
(l) Renewal while under suspension or disbarment. An individual who is ineligible to practice before the Internal Revenue Service by virtue of disciplinary action under this part is required to conform to the requirements for renewal of enrollment or registration before the individual's eligibility is restored.
(m) Enrolled actuaries. The enrollment and renewal of enrollment of actuaries authorized to practice under paragraph (d) of § 10.3 are governed by the regulations of the Joint Board for the Enrollment of Actuaries at 20 CFR 901.1 through 901.72.
(n) Effective/applicability date. This section is applicable to enrollment or registration effective beginning August 2, 2011.
[T.D. 9527, 76 FR 32302, June 3, 2011]

sections.title: Sanctions
sections.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 31 CFR § 10.50 — Sanctions for Circular 230 violations
sections.officialGuideLabel: IRS Publication 947 — Practice Before the IRS
sections.text:
§ 10.50 Sanctions.
(a) Authority to censure, suspend, or disbar. The Secretary of the Treasury, or delegate, after notice and an opportunity for a proceeding, may censure, suspend, or disbar any practitioner from practice before the Internal Revenue Service if the practitioner is shown to be incompetent or disreputable (within the meaning of § 10.51), fails to comply with any regulation in this part (under the prohibited conduct standards of § 10.52), or with intent to defraud, willfully and knowingly misleads or threatens a client or prospective client. Censure is a public reprimand.
(b) Authority to disqualify. The Secretary of the Treasury, or delegate, after due notice and opportunity for hearing, may disqualify any appraiser for a violation of these rules as applicable to appraisers.
(1) If any appraiser is disqualified pursuant to this subpart C, the appraiser is barred from presenting evidence or testimony in any administrative proceeding before the Department of Treasury or the Internal Revenue Service, unless and until authorized to do so by the Internal Revenue Service pursuant to § 10.81, regardless of whether the evidence or testimony would pertain to an appraisal made prior to or after the effective date of disqualification.
(2) Any appraisal made by a disqualified appraiser after the effective date of disqualification will not have any probative effect in any administrative proceeding before the Department of the Treasury or the Internal Revenue Service. An appraisal otherwise barred from admission into evidence pursuant to this section may be admitted into evidence solely for the purpose of determining the taxpayer's reliance in good faith on such appraisal.
(c) Authority to impose monetary penalty—(1) In general. (i) The Secretary of the Treasury, or delegate, after notice and an opportunity for a proceeding, may impose a monetary penalty on any practitioner who engages in conduct subject to sanction under paragraph (a) of this section.
(ii) If the practitioner described in paragraph (c)(1)(i) of this section was acting on behalf of an employer or any firm or other entity in connection with the conduct giving rise to the penalty, the Secretary of the Treasury, or delegate, may impose a monetary penalty on the employer, firm, or entity if it knew, or reasonably should have known, of such conduct.
(2) Amount of penalty. The amount of the penalty shall not exceed the gross income derived (or to be derived) from the conduct giving rise to the penalty.
(3) Coordination with other sanctions. Subject to paragraph (c)(2) of this section—
(i) Any monetary penalty imposed on a practitioner under this paragraph (c) may be in addition to or in lieu of any suspension, disbarment or censure and may be in addition to a penalty imposed on an employer, firm or other entity under paragraph (c)(1)(ii) of this section.
(ii) Any monetary penalty imposed on an employer, firm or other entity may be in addition to or in lieu of penalties imposed under paragraph (c)(1)(i) of this section.
(d) Authority to accept a practitioner's consent to sanction. The Internal Revenue Service may accept a practitioner's offer of consent to be sanctioned under § 10.50 in lieu of instituting or continuing a proceeding under § 10.60(a).
(e) Sanctions to be imposed. The sanctions imposed by this section shall take into account all relevant facts and circumstances.
(f) Effective/applicability date. This section is applicable to conduct occurring on or after August 2, 2011, except that paragraphs (a), (b)(2), and (e) apply to conduct occurring on or after September 26, 2007, and paragraph (c) applies to prohibited conduct that occurs after October 22, 2004.
[T.D. 9359, 72 FR 54549, Sept. 26, 2007, as amended by T.D. 9527, 76 FR 32308, June 3, 2011]

corpora.title: Title 26 CFR & IRC — IRS Special Enrollment Examination (SEE Parts 1–3)

parts.title: IRS SEE Part 1 — Individuals (Filing, Dependents, Assets, QBI & Gifts)

sections.title: Head of Household Filing Status & Abandoned Spouse Rules (IRC § 2(b))
sections.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 1.2-2 — Definitions and special rules (Head of Household)
sections.officialGuideLabel: IRS Publication 501 — Filing Status & Dependents
sections.text:
(b) Head of household (IRC § 2(b)). An individual is considered a head of a household only if the individual is unmarried (or considered unmarried under the abandoned spouse rule) at the close of the taxable year, is not a surviving spouse, and maintains as his or her home a household that constitutes for more than one-half of the taxable year the principal place of abode of a qualifying child or other qualifying dependent.
(b)(2) Special rule for a dependent parent. A taxpayer may qualify as head of household by maintaining a household that constitutes the principal place of abode of the taxpayer's father or mother if the taxpayer is entitled to claim the parent as a dependent, even if the parent does not live in the taxpayer's own home, provided the taxpayer pays more than half the cost of keeping up the parent's separate household for the entire year.
(c) Abandoned spouse exception. A married individual who lives apart from his or her spouse during the last 6 months of the taxable year, files a separate return, pays more than half the cost of maintaining a home that is the principal residence of a qualifying child for more than half the year, and can claim the child as a dependent is considered unmarried for Head of Household status.

sections.title: Qualifying Child vs. Qualifying Relative Dependent Rules (IRC § 152)
sections.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 1.152-1 — General definition of a dependent
sections.officialGuideLabel: IRS Publication 501 — Dependents & Filing Information
sections.text:
(a) Qualifying child tests (IRC § 152(c)). To be a taxpayer's qualifying child, an individual must meet the relationship test, age test (under age 19, or under age 24 if a full-time student for at least 5 calendar months, or permanently and totally disabled), residency test (same principal place of abode for more than half the year), joint return test, and support test: the child must not have provided more than one-half of his or her own support for the calendar year.
(b) Qualifying relative tests (IRC § 152(d)). Unlike a qualifying child, a qualifying relative is subject to a strict gross income ceiling and requires the taxpayer to provide more than one-half of the individual's total support for the calendar year. A non-relative (such as an unrelated friend) can qualify as a qualifying relative only if the individual lived with the taxpayer as a member of the household for the entire taxable year (all 12 months) and the relationship does not violate local law.

sections.title: Exclusion of Gain from Sale of Principal Residence (IRC § 121)
sections.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 1.121-1 — Exclusion of gain on principal residence
sections.officialGuideLabel: IRS Publication 523 — Selling Your Home
sections.text:
(a) In general (IRC § 121). A taxpayer may exclude up to $250,000 ($500,000 for certain married taxpayers filing jointly) of gain realized on the sale or exchange of property if, during the 5-year period ending on the date of the sale or exchange, the taxpayer owned and used the property as the taxpayer's principal residence for periods aggregating 2 years or more. The ownership and use periods need not be concurrent.
(d) Depreciation recapture limitation. The Section 121 exclusion does not apply to so much of the gain from the sale of a principal residence as does not exceed the portion of the depreciation adjustments attributable to periods after May 6, 1997 (unrecaptured Section 1250 gain from home office or rental depreciation). That post-May 6, 1997 depreciation recapture remains taxable even when total gain is below $250,000 / $500,000.

sections.title: Losses from Wash Sales of Stock or Securities (IRC § 1091)
sections.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 1.1091-1 — Losses from wash sales of stock or securities
sections.officialGuideLabel: IRS Publication 550 — Investment Income and Expenses
sections.text:
(a) Disallowance of loss (IRC § 1091). No deduction is allowed for any loss claimed to have been sustained from any sale or other disposition of shares of stock or securities where it appears that, within a period beginning 30 days before the date of such sale or disposition and ending 30 days after such date (a 61-day window), the taxpayer has acquired (by purchase or by an exchange on which the entire amount of gain or loss was recognized), or has entered into a contract or option so to acquire, substantially identical stock or securities.
(f) Basis and holding period of replacement stock. The disallowed wash sale loss is not permanently forfeited in a taxable account; instead, it is added to the basis of the newly acquired replacement stock or securities (IRC § 1091(d)), and the holding period of the sold shares is tacked onto the holding period of the replacement shares (IRC § 1223(3)). Note: Wash sale rules apply only to losses, never to gains.

sections.title: Qualified Business Income (QBI) 20% Deduction Operational Rules (IRC § 199A)
sections.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 1.199A-1 — QBI deduction operational rules
sections.officialGuideLabel: IRS Publication 17 — Your Federal Income Tax
sections.text:
(a) General operational rule (IRC § 199A). Non-corporate taxpayers (individuals, trusts, and estates) with qualified business income (QBI) from a domestic sole proprietorship, partnership, or S corporation may deduct up to 20 percent of QBI, limited overall to 20 percent of taxable income minus net capital gain. Income earned through a C corporation or by performing services as an employee (W-2 wages) does not qualify as QBI.
(d) Threshold and SSTB phase-out. For taxpayers whose taxable income is at or below the statutory threshold amount, neither the W-2 wage / UBIA of qualified property limitation nor the Specified Service Trade or Business (SSTB) exclusion applies. Once taxable income exceeds the phase-in range above the threshold, QBI from an SSTB (such as law, accounting, consulting, health, or financial services — excluding engineering and architecture) is completely disallowed, while non-SSTB businesses are capped by the greater of 50% of W-2 wages or 25% of W-2 wages plus 2.5% of UBIA of qualified property.

sections.title: Gift Tax Annual Exclusion, Present Interest & Direct Tuition/Medical Transfers (IRC § 2503)
sections.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 25.2503-2 — Exclusions from gifts
sections.officialGuideLabel: IRS.gov — Frequently Asked Questions on Gift Taxes
sections.text:
(a) Present interest requirement (IRC § 2503(b)). The federal gift tax annual exclusion applies per donee, per calendar year, ONLY to gifts of a present interest in property (an unrestricted right to the immediate use, possession, or enjoyment of property or the income from property). A gift of a future interest does not qualify for the annual exclusion and always requires filing Form 709 regardless of dollar amount.
(b) Unlimited exclusions for educational and medical transfers (IRC § 2503(e)). Qualified transfers paid directly to an educational organization for tuition (excluding room, board, or books) or directly to a healthcare provider for medical care on behalf of any individual are completely excluded from taxable gifts without reducing the annual exclusion or lifetime exemption.
(c) Gift splitting (IRC § 2513). Married spouses may elect to treat gifts made by one spouse to third parties as made one-half by each spouse, doubling the effective annual exclusion per donee, provided both spouses consent and file Form 709.

sections.title: Treatment of Partnership Liabilities — Recourse vs. Nonrecourse Basis (IRC § 752)
sections.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 1.752-1 — Treatment of partnership liabilities
sections.officialGuideLabel: IRS Publication 541 — Partnerships
sections.text:
(a) Definitions and outside basis impact (IRC § 752). Any increase in a partner's share of partnership liabilities is treated as a deemed contribution of money by the partner to the partnership, increasing outside basis. Conversely, any decrease in a partner's share of partnership liabilities is treated as a deemed distribution of money to the partner, reducing outside basis (and triggering capital gain if the deemed distribution exceeds outside basis).
(a)(1) Recourse liability. A partnership liability is a recourse liability to the extent that any partner or related person bears the economic risk of loss for that liability (typically allocated to general partners, not limited partners unless personally guaranteed).
(a)(2) Nonrecourse liability. A partnership liability is a nonrecourse liability to the extent that no partner or related person bears the economic risk of loss; nonrecourse liabilities are generally shared by both general and limited partners in accordance with their profit-sharing ratios, allowing limited partners to include a share of nonrecourse debt in outside basis.

sections.title: Section 179 Expensing Election, Business Income Limitation & Recapture (IRC § 179)
sections.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 1.179-1 — Election to expense depreciable assets
sections.officialGuideLabel: IRS Publication 946 — How To Depreciate Property
sections.text:
(b) Taxable income limitation and carryforward (IRC § 179(b)(3)). The Section 179 expense deduction for any taxable year cannot exceed the taxpayer's aggregate taxable income derived from the active conduct of any trade or business during the taxable year (including W-2 wages for an individual taxpayer, computed without regard to the Section 179 deduction). Any Section 179 amount disallowed solely by the taxable income limitation is carried forward indefinitely to succeeding taxable years (unlike a dollar phase-out reduction from excess property placed in service, which is permanently lost from Section 179 and recovered through MACRS depreciation).
(e) Recapture upon drop to 50% or less business use. If Section 179 property is not used predominantly (more than 50 percent) in a trade or business at any time before the end of the property's recovery period, the taxpayer must recapture as ordinary income the excess of the Section 179 deduction claimed over the MACRS depreciation that would have been allowable.

sections.title: Cash Method Accounting Limitation & Gross Receipts Test (IRC § 448)
sections.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 1.448-2 — Limitation on use of the cash method
sections.officialGuideLabel: IRS Publication 538 — Accounting Periods and Methods
sections.text:
(a) General limitation (IRC § 448(a)). Except as otherwise provided, a C corporation, a partnership that has a C corporation as a partner, or a tax shelter may not compute taxable income under the cash receipts and disbursements method of accounting.
(b) Small business taxpayer exception (IRC § 448(c)). A C corporation or partnership with a C corporation partner may use the cash method if it is not a tax shelter and meets the Section 448(c) gross receipts test: its average annual gross receipts for the 3-taxable-year period ending with the taxable year immediately preceding the current taxable year do not exceed the inflation-adjusted threshold ($25 million base indexed annually).
(c) Absolute bar for tax shelters. A tax shelter (including a syndicate where more than 35% of losses are allocated to limited partners or limited entrepreneurs) is strictly prohibited from using the cash method regardless of how low its annual gross receipts are.

sections.title: C Corporation Distributions — Current E&P, Accumulated E&P & Return of Capital (IRC § 301 / § 316)
sections.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 1.316-2 — Sources of corporate distributions (E&P)
sections.officialGuideLabel: IRS Publication 542 — Corporations

sections.title: Like-Kind Exchanges of Real Property — 45/180-Day & Boot Rules (IRC § 1031)
sections.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 1.1031(a)-1 — Like-kind exchanges of real property
sections.officialGuideLabel: IRS.gov — Like-Kind Exchanges (Real Estate Tax Tips)
sections.text:
(a) Real property limitation (Post-TCJA IRC § 1031). Nonrecognition of gain or loss under Section 1031 applies strictly to exchanges of real property held for productive use in a trade or business or for investment for like-kind real property. Personal property (such as machinery, vehicles, artwork, or cryptocurrency), inventory, stocks, bonds, and partnership interests do NOT qualify for Section 1031 deferral.
(b) Deferred exchange deadlines (IRC § 1031(a)(3)). In a deferred exchange, replacement real property must be (1) identified in writing within 45 calendar days after the transfer of the relinquished property, and (2) received by the earlier of 180 calendar days after the transfer or the due date (including extensions) of the taxpayer's return for that year.
(c) Boot recognition rule. If the taxpayer receives cash or other non-like-kind property (boot, including net mortgage relief), gain is recognized to the extent of the LESSER of realized gain or the fair market value of net boot received; losses are never recognized in a Section 1031 exchange.

parts.title: IRS SEE Part 3 — Representation, Statutes of Limitation, CDP & Penalties

sections.title: Power of Attorney (Form 2848) vs. Tax Information Authorization (Form 8821)
sections.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 601.504 — Requirements for filing power of attorney
sections.officialGuideLabel: IRS.gov — About Form 2848 (Power of Attorney)
sections.text:
(a) Power of Attorney required for representation (Form 2848). A Form 2848 (Power of Attorney and Declaration of Representative) is required when a taxpayer authorizes a recognized representative (such as an attorney, CPA, or Enrolled Agent) to represent and advocate for the taxpayer before the IRS, execute waivers or closing agreements, receive notices, or sign a return when specifically authorized.
(b) Tax Information Authorization distinction (Form 8821). By contrast, Form 8821 authorizes any designated individual, corporation, firm, or organization ONLY to inspect and receive confidential tax information for the specified tax matters and periods. Form 8821 does NOT authorize the appointee to advocate the taxpayer's position, execute waivers, or otherwise represent the taxpayer before the IRS.

sections.title: Statute of Limitations on Assessment — 3-Year General vs. 6-Year >25% Omission (IRC § 6501)
sections.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 301.6501(e)-1 — Omission from return (6-year period)
sections.officialGuideLabel: IRS Publication 556 — Examination of Returns & Limitations
sections.text:
(a) General 3-year and extended 6-year assessment periods (IRC § 6501). Generally, the IRS must assess tax within 3 years after the later of the date the return was actually filed or the original due date of the return.
(a)(1) Substantial omission of gross income (6-year statute). If a taxpayer omits from gross income an amount properly includible therein that is in excess of 25 percent of the amount of gross income stated in the return, the tax may be assessed at any time within 6 years after the return was filed. Overstating deductions (without omitting gross income >25%) does NOT trigger the 6-year statute.
(c) Unlimited statute of limitations. In the case of a false or fraudulent return with the intent to evade tax, or failure to file a return, the tax may be assessed at any time (no statute of limitations runs).

sections.title: Collection Due Process (CDP) Hearing Request Within 30 Days of Final Levy Notice (IRC § 6330)
keywords: Final Notice of Intent to Levy
sections.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 301.6330-1 — Notice and hearing prior to levy (CDP)
sections.officialGuideLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 301.6320-1 — Hearing upon Notice of Federal Tax Lien
sections.text:
(b) Right to a CDP hearing (IRC § 6330). Before the IRS may levy on any property or right to property, the IRS must notify the taxpayer in writing of the right to request a Collection Due Process (CDP) hearing before the Independent Office of Appeals. The taxpayer must submit a written request (Form 12153) within 30 calendar days beginning on the day after the date of the Final Notice of Intent to Levy.
(e) Suspension of levy and Tax Court appeal rights. A timely CDP hearing request generally suspends IRS levy action during the hearing and preserves the taxpayer's statutory right to petition the U.S. Tax Court within 30 days of an adverse Notice of Determination. A request filed after 30 days (within 1 year) qualifies only for an Equivalent Hearing, which does NOT preserve Tax Court judicial review rights.

sections.title: Paid Preparer Due Diligence Requirements & Form 8867 (IRC § 6695(g))
sections.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 1.6695-2 — Paid preparer due diligence requirements
sections.officialGuideLabel: IRS.gov — About Form 8867 (Due Diligence Checklist)
sections.text:
(a) Covered credits and filing status (IRC § 6695(g)). A paid tax return preparer must satisfy four strict due diligence requirements (completion and submission of Form 8867, computation of credit/status, knowledge requirement with reasonable inquiries, and 3-year record retention) for every return claiming any of four benefits: (1) Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), (2) Child Tax Credit / Additional Child Tax Credit / Credit for Other Dependents (CTC/ACTC/ODC), (3) American Opportunity Tax Credit (AOTC), or (4) Head of Household (HOH) filing status.
(b)(4) Record retention and per-failure penalty stacking. The preparer must retain Form 8867, worksheets, and copies of client-provided reliance documents for 3 years from the later of the return due date or filing date. Penalties under IRC § 6695(g) are assessed separately for EACH covered benefit on the same return (meaning up to four separate penalties on a single return).

sections.title: 20% Accuracy-Related Penalty — Negligence & Substantial Understatement (IRC § 6662)
sections.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 1.6662-3 — Negligence or disregard of rules
sections.officialGuideLabel: IRS.gov — Accuracy-Related Penalty (IRC § 6662)
sections.text:
(a) General 20% accuracy-related penalty (IRC § 6662). A 20 percent penalty applies to the portion of any underpayment of tax attributable to negligence or disregard of rules or regulations, or to any substantial understatement of income tax.
(b) Substantial understatement threshold for individuals (IRC § 6662(d)). For an individual taxpayer, an understatement of income tax is substantial if it exceeds the GREATER of 10 percent of the tax required to be shown on the return or $5,000 (5 percent or $5,000 if claiming the Section 199A QBI deduction).
(c) Defenses and non-stacking. Under IRC § 6664(c), no accuracy-related penalty applies to any portion of an underpayment where the taxpayer acted with reasonable cause and in good faith. In addition, an understatement is reduced by items supported by substantial authority or by reasonable basis coupled with adequate disclosure (Form 8275), and accuracy-related penalties under § 6662 do not stack on the same portion of an underpayment.

questions.stem: A freight forwarder selects broker Vance to handle entries for Cascade Imports and will collect the brokerage charges. Cascade has given no written waiver. What must the parties do under 19 CFR § 111.36(c) for Vance to compensate the forwarder for this referral?

options.text: A licensed customs broker is strictly prohibited under all circumstances from sharing fees or paying referral compensation to an unlicensed person or freight forwarder.

Vance may compensate the freight forwarder provided she obtains prior written approval from the Center of Excellence and Expertise (CEE) Director and caps the referral fee at 10% of the brokerage charge.
Vance may compensate the freight forwarder only if Cascade purchases the goods on a Delivered Duty Paid (DDP) basis and the forwarder acts as the Importer of Record.

Give Cascade advance notice of the selected broker’s name. Vance must send her charges directly to Cascade, obtain the customs power of attorney directly from the importer of record, preserve direct communication, and comply with the other broker regulations.
Vance may compensate the freight forwarder provided the forwarder rebates at least 50% of the referral commission back to the importer as a volume discount.

questions.goldenQuote: the name of the broker selected by the forwarder
questions.shortestPathHint: 19 CFR -> Part 111 -> § 111.36 (Relations with unlicensed persons)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Look for the specific regulatory exception to the general rule against fee-splitting with unlicensed persons when the unlicensed party is a freight forwarder.
Open 19 CFR § 111.36(c) and identify who selected the broker.
Look for the billing rule when the forwarder collects the charges. Then check who must grant the power of attorney.

explanation.correctReasoning: Either party may give the importer advance notice of the selected broker. When the forwarder collects and there is no written waiver, the broker sends a copy of the charges directly to the importer. Direct execution of the power of attorney and freedom to communicate with the broker are also required. When the broker collects, a different itemized billing rule applies.

distractors.A: Section 111.36(c) permits referral compensation when its conditions are met.
distractors.B: Incorrect because CBP regulations do not require CEE Director approval or impose a 10% percentage cap on freight forwarder referral fees.
distractors.C: Incorrect because DDP terms apply to the exception in § 111.36(a) regarding employment by an unlicensed intermediary, not the referral compensation requirements in § 111.36(c).
distractors.D: CORRECT: Accurately states the cumulative requirements of 19 CFR § 111.36(c)(1)–(4).
distractors.E: A rebate does not satisfy the notice, billing and direct power of attorney requirements.

questions.stem: While reviewing shipping documents prior to filing a consumption entry for client Global Auto Parts Inc., licensed customs broker David Chen discovers an email attachment showing that the foreign seller issued two separate invoices for the same shipment: a 'Customs Invoice' for $45,000 and a secret 'Supplemental Tooling & Price Adjustment Invoice' for $30,000 that Global Auto Parts wired separately to the seller's bank account. When Chen contacts Global Auto Parts' import manager, the manager instructs Chen to file the entry declaring only the $45,000 invoice and delete the supplemental invoice email. Under 19 CFR § 111.32, what is Broker Chen legally required to do?

options.text: File the entry at $45,000 as instructed by the principal under the Power of Attorney, because the Importer of Record bears sole legal liability for valuation accuracy under 19 U.S.C. 1484.
File the entry at $45,000 to avoid General Order storage fees, and then file a Post Summary Correction (PSC) within 180 days without informing the client.
Refuse to file the known false entry. Advise the client promptly about the omission and corrective action, and keep a record of that advice.
Immediately confiscate the importer's merchandise, arrest the import manager, and assess a $30,000 civil penalty on behalf of CBP.
Provide oral advice only over the telephone so that no discoverable paper trail exists, and continue filing entries for the client using the lower invoice values.

questions.goldenQuote: known by such broker to be false
questions.shortestPathHint: 19 CFR -> Part 111 -> § 111.32 (False information)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): A licensed customs broker is strictly prohibited from filing any document known to be false and has an affirmative regulatory duty when discovering client noncompliance or omission.
Locate § 111.32 on false information. For advice about a client error, consult § 111.39(c).
Separate the decision whether to file from the corrective advice you must give the client.

explanation.correctReasoning: Section 111.32 prohibits filing or helping file a document the broker knows is false. Section 111.39(c) requires prompt advice on the error and corrective action and a record of that communication. If representation later ends because the client tried to use the broker to defraud the U.S. government, § 111.32 also requires reporting that separation.

distractors.A: Filing a known false document violates § 111.32.
distractors.B: An intention to amend later does not permit a knowingly false filing.
distractors.C: The broker refuses the false filing and records the corrective advice.
distractors.D: A customs broker is a private licensee, not a federal law enforcement officer, and has no authority to confiscate cargo, make arrests, or assess CBP penalties.
distractors.E: Continuing to file the false entry violates § 111.32. Section 111.39(c) also requires keeping a record of corrective advice.

questions.stem: A licensed broker keeps original entry files and revoked powers of attorney, including electronic records. Its designated recordkeeping contact changes. A separate modernized drawback claim has liquidated. Which recordkeeping and contact practices should the broker apply?

options.text: Keep originals anywhere in North America and destroy a revoked power of attorney after one year.

Keep originals in the U.S. customs territory. Keep ordinary entry records at least five years from entry, and a revoked power of attorney and its revocation letter for five years from revocation or the end of active-client status, whichever is later. Keep drawback support three years from claim liquidation. Keep the designated contact current in CBP’s authorized EDI system.
Retain all records only until entry liquidation. Report the new contact in the next triennial status report.
Keep originals only in the district of entry and retain revoked powers of attorney indefinitely.
Keep electronic originals solely outside the U.S. customs territory and keep drawback support for one year after export.

questions.goldenQuote: must be retained for at least 5 years after the date of entry
socraticHints: Identify the record type first.
For a revoked power compare two five-year end dates.

explanation.correctReasoning: Section 111.23 sets the location and ordinary retention rules. Section 111.21(d) requires current contact information in authorized EDI, with written notice to the processing Center when EDI is unavailable. The modernized drawback certification uses three years from liquidation of the claim.

distractors.A: North America extends beyond the U.S. customs territory. The retention period for a revoked power of attorney is longer.
distractors.B: Section 111.23 sets the location and ordinary retention rules. Section 111.21(d) requires current contact information in authorized EDI, with written notice to the processing Center when EDI is unavailable. The modernized drawback certification uses three years from liquidation of the claim.
distractors.C: Ordinary entry retention runs from entry. The designated contact information must remain current.
distractors.D: The geographical rule applies across the U.S. customs territory. A revoked power of attorney has a defined retention period.
distractors.E: The location rule includes electronic originals. Drawback claim support runs from claim liquidation.

questions.stem: CBP timely demands redelivery of two shipments. The importer misses the deadline specified in each demand. FDA refused admission of restricted laser devices appraised at $60,000. An ordinary shipment of improperly marked tableware is appraised at $40,000 and had $3,600 in estimated duties and fees. No special bond provision or alternative damages rule applies. What liquidated damages follow for the two redelivery defaults?

options.text: $30,000 per shipment.

questions.goldenQuote: three times the value of the merchandise involved in the default
socraticHints: Separate the appraised value from estimated duties.
Classify each shipment as restricted or ordinary before applying the multiplier.

explanation.correctReasoning: The restricted devices produce $180,000 at three times $60,000. The ordinary tableware produces $40,000 at its appraised value. Paragraph (n)(2) uses the value determined by CBP. The estimated duties are a separate obligation.

distractors.A: The restricted devices trigger the three-times-value measure.
distractors.B: The restricted devices produce $180,000 at three times $60,000. The ordinary tableware produces $40,000 at its appraised value. Paragraph (n)(2) uses the value determined by CBP. The estimated duties are a separate obligation.
distractors.C: The restricted multiplier applies only to the restricted merchandise here. Estimate-based additions do not enter this damages calculation.
distractors.D: The general redelivery default uses the merchandise value and classification.
distractors.E: Adding the tableware’s $3,600 in estimated duties overstates the damages for redelivery.

questions.stem: A national permit holder receives a client’s duty payment after the government due date, retains unrefunded excess client funds, and hires an employee on April 1. How soon must it transmit the late payment, account to the client in writing for the excess, and report the hire?

options.text: Ten working days after receipt, 60 days after receipt, and 60 days after hiring.
Five working days after receipt, 60 calendar days after receipt, and 30 calendar days from the start of employment.
Two working days after receipt, 30 calendar days after receipt, and 30 days after probation ends.
Five calendar days after receipt, 45 calendar days after receipt, and 30 days after completion of the first month.
Fifteen calendar days after receipt, one year after receipt, and with the next status report.

questions.goldenQuote: within 5 working days from receipt by the broker
questions.shortestPathHint: Read § 111.29(a) and the new-employee rule in § 111.28(b)(2).
socraticHints: Distinguish working days from calendar days.
Read § 111.29(a) and the new-employee rule in § 111.28(b)(2).
Count the hire period once, beginning at the start of employment.

explanation.correctReasoning: Section 111.29(a) sets the payment and accounting periods. Section 111.28(b)(2) starts the reporting clock on the employment start date, so the April 1 hire is reportable by May 1.

distractors.A: The late payment and new-hire periods are too long.
distractors.B: Section 111.29(a) sets the payment and accounting periods. Section 111.28(b)(2) starts the reporting clock on the employment start date, so the April 1 hire is reportable by May 1.
distractors.C: A probation period does not start the reporting clock. The financial deadlines also differ.
distractors.D: The payment period uses working days. The employment clock begins on the start date.
distractors.E: The broker must act on each event within its specific regulatory period.

questions.stem: A container vessel carrying non-quota commercial machinery arrives within the port limits of Savannah, GA and lands its cargo on Monday, November 2. On Tuesday, November 3, the licensed customs broker transmits the entry documentation (CBP Form 3461 electronic equivalent) without an entry summary and without requesting an immediate time-of-entry election upon filing. On Wednesday, November 4, CBP authorizes the release of the merchandise. Wednesday, November 11 is Veterans Day (a federal holiday). Under 19 CFR § 141.68 and § 142.12, what is the 'time of entry' for this shipment, and what is the final deadline for the broker to file the Entry Summary (CBP Form 7501) with estimated duties attached without incurring liquidated damages?

options.text: Time of entry is Monday, November 2; the Entry Summary is due no later than Tuesday, November 17 (15 calendar days after landing).
Time of entry is Tuesday, November 3; the Entry Summary is due no later than Tuesday, November 17 (10 working days after filing CBP Form 3461).
Time of entry is Wednesday, November 4; the Entry Summary is due no later than Wednesday, November 18 (10 working days after time of entry, including Veterans Day).

Time of entry is Wednesday, November 4; the Entry Summary is due no later than Thursday, November 19 (10 working days after time of entry, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and the Veterans Day federal holiday).
Time of entry is Thursday, November 19 (when the Entry Summary is filed); the Entry Summary is due within 30 calendar days after release.

questions.goldenQuote: within 10 working days after the time of entry
questions.shortestPathHint: 19 CFR -> Part 142 -> § 142.12 (Time for filing entry summary)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): First determine the 'time of entry' under 19 CFR § 141.68(a)(1) when CBP Form 3461 is filed without an entry summary and without a special filing-time request.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 19 CFR Part 142 -> § 142.12(b) and (c) to see the exact deadline for filing Entry Summary (CBP Form 7501) after the time of entry.

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Count 10 WORKING days starting on the day AFTER CBP authorizes release (Release = Wed, Nov 4 -> Day 1 = Thu, Nov 5). Exclude Sat/Sun (Nov 7–8), Wed Nov 11 (Veterans Day federal holiday), and Sat/Sun (Nov 14–15).

explanation.correctReasoning: First, under 19 CFR § 141.68(a)(1), when entry documentation (CBP Form 3461) is filed without an entry summary and the importer has not requested time of entry at filing, the 'time of entry' is the time CBP authorizes the release of the merchandise—here, Wednesday, November 4. Second, under 19 CFR § 142.12(b) and (c), the Entry Summary (CBP Form 7501) with estimated duties attached must be filed within 10 working days after the time of entry, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and federal holidays. Counting working days starting the day after November 4: Day 1 = Thu Nov 5; Day 2 = Fri Nov 6; [Sat Nov 7 & Sun Nov 8 excluded]; Day 3 = Mon Nov 9; Day 4 = Tue Nov 10; [Wed Nov 11 excluded for Veterans Day federal holiday]; Day 5 = Thu Nov 12; Day 6 = Fri Nov 13; [Sat Nov 14 & Sun Nov 15 excluded]; Day 7 = Mon Nov 16; Day 8 = Tue Nov 17; Day 9 = Wed Nov 18; Day 10 = Thursday, November 19.

distractors.A: Confuses the 10-working-day Entry Summary deadline (§ 142.12(b)) with the 15-calendar-day initial entry filing window after landing before merchandise goes to General Order (§ 142.2(a)).
distractors.B: Erroneously uses the date CBP Form 3461 was submitted (Nov 3) as the time of entry without an importer election under § 141.68(a)(2) and fails to exclude Veterans Day.
distractors.C: Correctly identifies Wednesday, November 4 as the time of entry, but fails to exclude Wednesday, November 11 (Veterans Day federal holiday) when counting 10 working days.
distractors.D: CORRECT: Time of entry is Wednesday, November 4 (release authorization), and Day 10 of working days (excluding weekends and Veterans Day) is Thursday, November 19.
distractors.E: Confuses standard consumption entry release (§ 141.68(a)) with Immediate Delivery release (§ 141.68(c)), where time of entry is when the entry summary is filed, and states a non-existent 30-day deadline.

questions.stem: Sonora Industrial Supply Co. imports precision ball bearings from a manufacturer in Monterrey, Mexico, destined for the Port of Laredo, TX. The Mexican seller issues a commercial invoice written entirely in Spanish that states a single lump-sum CIF Laredo price in Mexican Pesos (MXN), without separately itemizing ocean/rail freight or insurance, and omits the $9,500 value of specialized hardening dies that Sonora purchased in Germany and furnished free of charge to the Mexican plant. Under 19 CFR § 141.86, which of the following statements accurately describes the legal sufficiency of this commercial invoice for CBP entry purposes?

options.text: The invoice is fully compliant because invoices from USMCA countries (Mexico and Canada) may be submitted in Spanish or French without translation, and foreign assists never need to be disclosed on a commercial invoice.

The invoice is deficient because § 141.86 requires every commercial invoice to be in the English language (or have attached an accurate English translation), to itemize all charges upon the merchandise by name and amount (including freight, insurance, commission, and packing), and to disclose all goods or services furnished for production not included in the invoice price (such as foreign-sourced dies/assists), while stating the purchase price in the currency of purchase.
The invoice is deficient solely because all commercial invoices presented to CBP must state the purchase price exclusively in U.S. Dollars (USD) converted by the foreign seller prior to shipment.
The invoice is compliant with respect to omitting the German dies, because only goods or services furnished inside the United States must be disclosed under § 141.86(a)(11).
The invoice does not need to state the port of entry, country of origin, or quantities in weights and measures if the shipment is valued under $250,000.

questions.goldenQuote: must be in the English language, or must have attached thereto an accurate English translation
questions.shortestPathHint: 19 CFR -> Part 141 -> § 141.86 (Contents of invoice)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Check the mandatory data elements required on every commercial invoice presented for U.S. customs entry, including currency, itemized charges, assist disclosures, and language requirements.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 19 CFR Part 141 -> § 141.86 and inspect paragraphs (a)(5), (a)(8), (a)(11), and (d).

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Under § 141.86(a)(5), stating the purchase price in the currency of purchase (MXN) is actually required! However, the invoice violates § 141.86(a)(8) (unitemized freight/insurance), § 141.86(a)(11) (omission of the German dies assist), and § 141.86(d) (must be in English or have an accurate English translation attached).

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 19 CFR § 141.86(a) and (d), a commercial invoice must satisfy eleven general content requirements plus the English language rule: (1) Under § 141.86(d), the invoice and all attachments must be in the English language or have attached thereto an accurate translation into English; (2) Under § 141.86(a)(8), all charges upon the merchandise (including freight, insurance, commissions, and containers/packing) must be itemized by name and amount; (3) Under § 141.86(a)(11), all goods or services furnished for the production of the merchandise not included in the invoice price (such as the German hardening dies assist) must be set forth on the invoice (only goods/services furnished in the U.S. are excluded); and (4) Under § 141.86(a)(5), the purchase price is properly stated in the currency of purchase (here, MXN).

distractors.A: Incorrect because there is no USMCA exemption from the English translation requirement in § 141.86(d) or the assist disclosure rule in § 141.86(a)(11).
distractors.B: CORRECT: Accurately identifies the English translation requirement (§ 141.86(d)), itemized charges rule (§ 141.86(a)(8)), foreign assist disclosure rule (§ 141.86(a)(11)), and currency-of-purchase rule (§ 141.86(a)(5)).
distractors.C: Incorrect because § 141.86(a)(5) explicitly requires the invoice to set forth the purchase price in the currency of the purchase (CBP converts foreign currency using quarterly/daily Federal Reserve rates under 19 CFR Part 159).
distractors.D: Reverses the rule in § 141.86(a)(11): foreign assists (like the German dies) MUST be disclosed, whereas goods or services furnished in the United States are excluded.
distractors.E: Incorrect because port of entry (§ 141.86(a)(1)), quantities in weights and measures (§ 141.86(a)(4)), and country of origin (§ 141.86(a)(10)) are mandatory on all commercial invoices.

questions.stem: Ordinary commercial watches land from an aircraft. Entry is required. The goods are neither perishable nor subject to an expedited disposal rule. Which timetable controls entry and the ordinary general-order period?

options.text: Ten working days after landing and three months from delivery to the warehouse.
Enter within 15 calendar days after landing. If the watches remain without entry, general-order procedures apply. The ordinary period before sale expires six months from importation.
Enter within 30 calendar days after landing. The six months run from appraisal.
Enter within five working days after departure from the foreign airport. The goods are sold immediately when the deadline passes.
Enter within 20 working days after arrival. General order lasts one year from importation.

questions.goldenQuote: within 15 calendar days after landing from a vessel, aircraft or vehicle
questions.shortestPathHint: Start with § 142.2(a), then read §§ 127.1, 127.4 and 127.11.
socraticHints: Find the ordinary entry deadline for landed cargo.
Start with § 142.2(a), then read §§ 127.1, 127.4 and 127.11.
Anchor the six months to importation.

explanation.correctReasoning: Section 142.2(a) sets the 15-day entry period. Sections 127.1 and 127.4 govern general order and its six months from importation. Section 127.11 addresses when unpaid goods remaining in Customs custody are unclaimed and abandoned.

distractors.A: The initial deadline is 15 calendar days and the general-order period runs from importation.
distractors.B: Section 142.2(a) sets the 15-day entry period. Sections 127.1 and 127.4 govern general order and its six months from importation. Section 127.11 addresses when unpaid goods remaining in Customs custody are unclaimed and abandoned.
distractors.C: Both the entry deadline and the starting point for the general-order period are wrong.
distractors.D: The landing starts the entry clock. Ordinary goods have a general-order period before sale.
distractors.E: The periods are 15 calendar days and six months.

questions.stem: On October 1, 2025 a corporation and a general partnership grant customs powers of attorney. The corporation imports a $650 commercial shipment of phone cases; the partnership imports $700 of steel rods subject to antidumping duties. Both are ordinary non-postal shipments, with no special exemption. What terms may the powers have, and can either shipment claim the former low-value exemption under 19 U.S.C. 1321(a)(2)(C)?

options.text: Both powers may be unlimited, and both shipments qualify.
The corporate power may be unlimited; the partnership power is limited to two years from execution. Neither shipment qualifies for the suspended low-value treatment on that date.
Both powers expire after five years and only the rods qualify.
