questions.stem:
A presidential proclamation modifies the HTSUS to increase the Column 1 duty rate on certain alloy steel valves from 2.5% to 6.0% effective at 12:01 a.m. on Thursday, October 15. A container vessel carrying three separate shipments of these alloy steel valves arrives within the port limits of Los Angeles-Long Beach and lands its cargo on Tuesday, October 13:
• Shipment 1 (Standard Entry Without Entry Summary — No Filing-Time Election): On Wednesday, October 14, the broker transmits CBP Form 3461 entry documentation without an entry summary and without requesting time of entry at filing; CBP authorizes release on Thursday, October 15.
• Shipment 2 ('Live Entry' — Entry Summary Serving as Entry and Entry Summary): On Wednesday, October 14 (after the vessel has arrived within the port limits), the broker files the Entry Summary (CBP Form 7501) in proper form serving as both entry and entry summary with estimated duties attached; CBP authorizes physical release on Thursday, October 15.
• Shipment 3 (Immediate Delivery Procedure): Released on Wednesday, October 14 under a special permit for Immediate Delivery (CBP Form 3461), and the Entry Summary (CBP Form 7501) with estimated duties attached is filed on Wednesday, October 21.

Under 19 CFR § 141.68(a), (b), (c), and (e) (§ 141.69), what is the legal 'time of entry' and applicable duty rate (2.5% vs. 6.0%) for Shipment 1, Shipment 2, and Shipment 3?

options.text: All three shipments have a time of entry of Tuesday, October 13 (the date the vessel arrived within port limits) and are subject to the 2.5% duty rate.

Shipment 1's time of entry is Thursday, October 15 (when CBP authorizes release, resulting in the 6.0% rate); Shipment 2's time of entry is Wednesday, October 14 (when the live Entry Summary is filed in proper form with estimated duties attached after arrival within port limits, locking in the 2.5% rate); and Shipment 3's time of entry is Wednesday, October 21 (when the Entry Summary is filed in proper form with estimated duties attached after Immediate Delivery release, resulting in the 6.0% rate).
Shipment 1 and Shipment 3 lock in the 2.5% duty rate on Wednesday, October 14, whereas Shipment 2 is subject to the 6.0% duty rate because physical release occurred on Thursday, October 15.
All three shipments are subject to the 6.0% duty rate because CBP authorized physical cargo release for Shipments 1 and 2 on October 15 and Entry Summary for Shipment 3 was filed on October 21.
Shipment 1's time of entry is Wednesday, October 14 (2.5% rate); Shipment 2's time of entry is Thursday, October 15 (6.0% rate); and Shipment 3's time of entry is Wednesday, October 14 (2.5% rate).

questions.goldenQuote: the time the entry summary is filed in proper form with estimated duties attached
questions.shortestPathHint: 19 CFR -> Part 141 -> § 141.68 (Time of entry)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Under 19 CFR § 141.68(e) (§ 141.69), merchandise is subject to the rate of duty in effect at the legal 'time of entry', which differs depending on whether entry is made via standard CBP Form 3461, Live Entry Summary (CBP Form 7501), or Immediate Delivery.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 19 CFR Part 141 -> § 141.68 and compare paragraphs (a)(1), (b), and (c).

Hint 3 (Trap Check): For Shipment 1 (standard 3461 with no election), time of entry is when CBP authorizes release (Oct 15 -> 6.0%). For Shipment 2 (Live Entry Summary 7501 with estimated duties attached after arrival), time of entry is the time of filing (Oct 14 -> 2.5%) even though release happens the next day! For Shipment 3 (Immediate Delivery), time of entry is when the Entry Summary 7501 is filed with duties attached (Oct 21 -> 6.0%).

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 19 CFR § 141.68(e) (§ 141.69), imported merchandise is subject to the rate of duty in effect at the 'time of entry' determined under § 141.68: (1) For Shipment 1, under § 141.68(a)(1), when entry documentation (CBP Form 3461) is filed without an entry summary and without an importer request on the entry documentation for time of entry at filing, the time of entry is the time CBP authorizes release (Thursday, October 15 -> 6.0% duty rate); (2) For Shipment 2, under § 141.68(b), when an entry summary (CBP Form 7501) serves as both entry and entry summary ('live entry'), the time of entry is the time the entry summary is filed in proper form with estimated duties attached, provided the merchandise has arrived within the port limits (Wednesday, October 14 -> 2.5% duty rate); and (3) For Shipment 3, under § 141.68(c), when merchandise is released under the immediate delivery procedure, the time of entry is the time the entry summary is filed in proper form with estimated duties attached (Wednesday, October 21 -> 6.0% duty rate).

distractors.A: Vessel arrival date is not the time of entry unless the importer submits entry documentation prior to arrival AND explicitly requests arrival time on the entry documentation under § 141.68(a)(3).
distractors.B: CORRECT: Shipment 1 = Oct 15 (6.0% under § 141.68(a)(1)); Shipment 2 = Oct 14 (2.5% under § 141.68(b) live entry summary); Shipment 3 = Oct 21 (6.0% under § 141.68(c) immediate delivery).
distractors.C: Reverses the outcomes of all three procedures under § 141.68.
distractors.D: Fails to recognize that a Live Entry Summary under § 141.68(b) establishes time of entry upon filing in proper form with estimated duties attached (Oct 14), prior to CBP release authorization.
distractors.E: Incorrectly treats Immediate Delivery release on Oct 14 as the time of entry; under § 141.68(c), Immediate Delivery time of entry occurs only when the Entry Summary is filed with estimated duties attached.

questions.goldenQuote: as a condition of the sale of the imported merchandise
questions.shortestPathHint: 19 CFR -> Part 152 -> § 152.103 (Transaction value: PAPP, Statutory Additions & Exclusions)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Start with the CIF invoice total ($115,000) and determine which international shipment charges must be deducted to arrive at the base Price Actually Paid or Payable (PAPP).

Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 19 CFR Part 152 -> § 152.103(b)(1) to check the five statutory additions to PAPP, and cross-reference § 152.102(a) to see which buyer-supplied items qualify as dutiable assists.

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Buying commissions ($4,000) and U.S.-undertaken engineering/design sketches ($6,000) are NEVER added! Add only the mold assist including its freight to the foreign factory ($8,000 + $500) and the condition-of-sale patent royalty ($3,500).

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 19 CFR § 152.103(a)(1) and (i)(1), international ocean freight ($11,000) and marine cargo insurance ($1,500) are excluded from the CIF price ($115,000) because they are separately itemized, yielding a base Price Actually Paid or Payable (PAPP) of $102,500 ($115,000 - $12,500). Next, under § 152.103(b)(1), we add: (1) the mold assist value of $8,500 ($8,000 acquisition cost + $500 freight to transport the mold to the foreign factory per § 152.102(a)(3)); and (2) the $3,500 patent royalty because the buyer is required to pay it as a condition of the sale for exportation to the U.S. under § 152.103(b)(1)(iv). The $4,000 buying commission is excluded (only selling commissions are added under § 152.103(b)(1)(ii)), and the $6,000 design work undertaken in the United States is excluded from the definition of an assist under § 152.102(a)(1)(iv) & (a)(2). Calculation: $102,500 + $8,500 + $3,500 = $114,500.

distractors.A: $102,500 is the net FOB Price Actually Paid or Payable ($115,000 - $11,000 freight - $1,500 insurance), but it omits the mandatory statutory additions for the mold assist ($8,500) and the condition-of-sale royalty ($3,500).
distractors.B: CORRECT ($114,500): Net PAPP of $102,500 + $8,500 mold assist (including transport to the factory) + $3,500 condition-of-sale royalty.
distractors.C: $118,500 erroneously includes the $4,000 bona fide buying commission. Under 19 CFR § 152.103(b)(1)(ii), only selling commissions incurred by the buyer are added to PAPP.
distractors.D: $120,500 erroneously includes the $6,000 design sketches created in Seattle. Under 19 CFR § 152.102(a)(1)(iv), engineering and design work is an assist only when undertaken OUTSIDE the United States.
distractors.E: $127,000 fails to deduct the separately itemized $11,000 international ocean freight and $1,500 marine cargo insurance from the CIF invoice price ($114,500 + $12,500).

questions.goldenQuote: undertaken elsewhere than in the United States
questions.shortestPathHint: 19 CFR -> Part 152 -> § 152.102 (Definitions: Assist, Related persons, Identical/Similar merchandise)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Evaluate each of the 5 items against the four exclusive categories of an 'assist' in 19 CFR § 152.102(a)(1) and the assist valuation rule in § 152.102(a)(3).
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 19 CFR Part 152 -> § 152.102(a) and check how foreign-undertaken engineering (Milan, Italy) differs from U.S.-undertaken engineering (Minneapolis, MN).

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Include Item 1 ($22,000 incorporated silicone tubing), Item 2 ($15,000 Italian engineering undertaken outside the U.S.), and Item 5 ($1,200 freight to transport the tubing assist to the factory). Exclude Item 3 (U.S.-domiciled engineering) and Item 4 (office A/C not used in production of the merchandise).

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 19 CFR § 152.102(a)(1)–(3), we evaluate each item: (1) The $22,000 biocompatible silicone tubing is an assist under § 152.102(a)(1)(i) because it is a material/component incorporated in the imported merchandise; (2) The $15,000 CAD/CAM engineering blueprints developed in Milan, Italy are an assist under § 152.102(a)(1)(iv) because they constitute engineering/design work undertaken OUTSIDE the United States and necessary for production; (3) The $18,000 engineering work performed in Minneapolis by U.S.-domiciled employees is explicitly EXCLUDED from being an assist under § 152.102(a)(1)(iv) and (a)(2); (4) The $12,000 administrative office air conditioner is NOT an assist because it is not a tool/die/mold used in production of the catheters nor consumed in production; and (5) The $1,200 air courier cost to transport the silicone tubing assist to the Costa Rican factory is added to the value of the assist under § 152.102(a)(3). Total dutiable assist value = $22,000 + $15,000 + $1,200 = $38,200.

distractors.A: $22,000 includes only the silicone tubing and omits both the foreign engineering blueprints ($15,000) and the freight to transport the tubing to the foreign plant ($1,200).
distractors.B: $37,000 includes the silicone tubing ($22,000) and the Italian engineering ($15,000) but forgets to add the $1,200 transportation cost of delivering the assist to the foreign place of production under § 152.102(a)(3).
distractors.C: CORRECT ($38,200): $22,000 incorporated tubing + $15,000 foreign engineering (Italy) + $1,200 assist transport cost to the factory.
distractors.D: $56,200 erroneously includes the $18,000 U.S.-based engineering work performed in Minneapolis, which is excluded under 19 CFR § 152.102(a)(1)(iv) and (a)(2).
distractors.E: $68,200 erroneously includes every single item, including U.S. engineering ($18,000) and non-production office air conditioning ($12,000).

questions.stem: During its own review CBP proposes to revoke an interpretive classification ruling issued three years ago. No court decision, change of law, exception to publication or extraordinary circumstance applies. The interested person makes no election for early application. Which notice and effective-date timetable governs?

options.text: Immediate revocation with no publication.

CBP publishes the proposal in the Customs Bulletin, allows 30 calendar days for written comment, publishes final action ordinarily within 30 calendar days after comments close, and applies the ordinary effective date 60 calendar days after the final publication.
CBP sends a private letter with ten working days of notice and no public comment.
CBP may never revoke a ruling more than one year old.

questions.stem: On March 10, 2024, Precision Optics Corp. imported 1,000 laser rangefinders classified under HTSUS subheading 9015.10.4000 ('Rangefinders: Electrical', duty rate 5% ad valorem; note that the 8-digit subheading 9015.10.40 description does NOT begin with the word 'Other'). The entered value was $200.00 per unit ($200,000 total), and Precision Optics paid $10,000.00 in customs duties ($10.00 duty per unit). On August 15, 2026, Precision Optics exported 1,000 unused domestic rangefinders to Germany that were never used in the United States and are also classified under HTSUS 9015.10.4000, but have a lower commercial export invoice value of $150.00 per unit ($150,000 total). Precision Optics timely files a TFTEA Unused Merchandise Substitution Drawback claim (19 U.S.C. 1313(j)(2)) in ACE designating the 1,000 imported units (ignoring MPF for this calculation). Under 19 CFR § 190.32, what is the maximum drawback duty refund allowable on this claim?

options.text: $0.00, because the exported rangefinders were domestically produced and have a different unit value than the imported rangefinders.

questions.goldenQuote: 99 percent of the lesser of
questions.shortestPathHint: 19 CFR -> Part 190 -> § 190.32 (Unused merchandise substitution drawback & 'lesser of' rule)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Under TFTEA Modernized Drawback, unused substitution (19 U.S.C. 1313(j)(2)) is based on matching 8-digit HTSUS classification, but the refund amount is subject to a statutory value comparison cap.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 19 CFR Part 190 -> § 190.32 and read paragraph (c) ('Amount of drawback — The "Lesser Of" Rule').

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Compare the duty paid on the imported units ($200,000 x 5% = $10,000) against the duty that would apply to the lower-valued substituted exported units ($150,000 x 5% = $7,500). Take the LESSER amount ($7,500) and multiply by the 99% drawback rate ($7,500 x 0.99)!

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 19 CFR § 190.32(a) and (b)(1), unused merchandise substitution drawback under 19 U.S.C. 1313(j)(2) is valid because both the designated imported merchandise and the substituted exported domestic merchandise are classified under the same 8-digit HTSUS subheading (9015.10.40, which does not begin with 'Other') and exportation occurred within 5 years of importation. However, under § 190.32(c) (the TFTEA 'Lesser Of' Rule), the drawback refund is capped at 99% of the LESSER of: (1) the duties paid on the designated imported merchandise ($200/unit x 1,000 units x 5% = $10,000.00), OR (2) the duties that would have applied to the substituted exported merchandise had it been imported at that rate ($150/unit x 1,000 units x 5% = $7,500.00). Since $7,500.00 is less than $10,000.00, we apply the 99% refund limit to $7,500.00: $7,500.00 x 0.99 = $7,425.00.

distractors.A: Incorrect because 19 CFR § 190.32(a) explicitly permits substituting domestic or imported merchandise classified under the same 8-digit HTSUS subheading regardless of price differences.
distractors.B: CORRECT ($7,425.00): 99% of the lesser duty amount ($150,000 substituted export value x 5% duty rate = $7,500.00 x 99% = $7,425.00).
distractors.C: $7,500.00 applies the 'lesser of' cap correctly ($150,000 x 5%) but forgets to reduce the refund by the mandatory 1% CBP retention (99% drawback limit).
distractors.D: $9,900.00 is 99% of the $10,000.00 duty paid on the imported merchandise, ignoring the mandatory 'lesser of' rule in 19 CFR § 190.32(c) when the substituted exported goods have a lower value.
distractors.E: $10,000.00 is 100% of the imported duty paid, ignoring both the 99% drawback limit and the § 190.32(c) 'lesser of' rule.

questions.stem: An importer designates duty-paid polymers imported November 16, 2021 for a complete, otherwise eligible modernized direct-identification manufacturing drawback claim. It exported the finished articles unused in June 2025. No extension or special destination limitation applies. What is the ordinary claim deadline, what is the claim-record period under the § 190.51 certification, and which charges are potentially eligible?

options.text: Five years after liquidation; one year of records; ordinary duties only.

November 16, 2026; three years from liquidation of the drawback claim; ordinary customs duties, merchandise processing fees, and harbor maintenance taxes can qualify. Antidumping and countervailing duties cannot.
Three years after export; retain records until export; all charges including antidumping duties qualify.
Five years after manufacture; retain records six months; only harbor maintenance taxes qualify.
180 days after export; retain records seven years; only countervailing duties qualify.

questions.goldenQuote: Harbor maintenance taxes
socraticHints: Distinguish importation, export and claim liquidation.
Locate the separate lines for MPF, harbor maintenance taxes and AD/CVD.

explanation.correctReasoning: Section 190.51(e)(1) runs five years from importation; its paragraph (a)(2)(xvi) certification measures three years from liquidation of the claim. Section 190.3(a) includes MPF and harbor maintenance taxes. Paragraph (b) excludes antidumping and countervailing duties.

distractors.A: The claim clock starts with the designated importation. The rules allow more than ordinary duties.
distractors.B: Section 190.51(e)(1) runs five years from importation; its paragraph (a)(2)(xvi) certification measures three years from liquidation of the claim. Section 190.3(a) includes MPF and harbor maintenance taxes. Paragraph (b) excludes antidumping and countervailing duties.
distractors.C: Export does not start the ordinary five-year claim clock. AD/CVD is excluded.
distractors.D: Manufacture does not start the filing period and eligible charges extend beyond harbor maintenance taxes.
distractors.E: Neither the timing nor the eligible charge is correct.

questions.stem:
Titan Printing Systems Inc. (an unrelated U.S. importer in Chicago, IL) purchases an industrial offset printing press from a manufacturer in Germany. The commercial invoice states a single turnkey delivered price of $450,000, which includes the following three post-importation items that are separately identified by name and dollar amount on the invoice:
• $28,000 for post-importation erection, assembly, calibration, and technical assistance performed at Titan's Chicago facility after the press is imported into the United States;
• $9,000 for post-importation U.S. domestic inland lowboy trucking from the Port of Newark, NJ to Chicago, IL; and
• $13,000 for U.S. customs duties and federal taxes currently payable on the imported press by reason of its importation.

In addition, outside the $450,000 invoice total, Titan incurred two separate payments:
• $6,500 paid by Titan to an export crating contractor in Hamburg for vacuum-sealed moisture-barrier wooden crates and packing labor required to pack the press for export; and
• $16,000 in patent license royalties that the sales contract requires Titan to pay to a Swiss patent holder as a condition of the sale of the printing press for exportation to the United States.

Under 19 CFR § 152.103(b) and (i), what is the correct transaction value (appraised value) of the imported printing press?
questions.goldenQuote: after its importation into the United States
questions.shortestPathHint: 19 CFR -> Part 152 -> § 152.103 (Transaction value: PAPP, Statutory Additions & Exclusions)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Deduct all separately identified post-importation exclusions from the $450,000 turnkey price under 19 CFR § 152.103(i), then add the mandatory statutory additions under § 152.103(b)(1).

Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 19 CFR Part 152 -> § 152.103 and inspect paragraph (i)(2)–(3) ('Exclusions from transaction value') and paragraph (b)(1)(i) & (iv) ('Additions to price actually paid or payable').

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Deduct $28,000 (post-importation assembly/technical assistance), $9,000 (post-importation U.S. inland freight), and $13,000 (U.S. customs duties/taxes) from $450,000 to get $400,000 net PAPP. Then add $6,500 (buyer-incurred export packing costs) and $16,000 (condition-of-sale patent royalty) = $422,500.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 19 CFR § 152.103(i)(2) and (3), transaction value does NOT include any of the following when separately identified from the price actually paid or payable: (1) reasonable costs incurred for construction, erection, assembly, maintenance, or technical assistance provided with respect to the merchandise AFTER its importation into the United States ($28,000); (2) transportation of the merchandise AFTER its importation into the United States ($9,000 U.S. domestic trucking); and (3) U.S. customs duties and federal taxes payable by reason of importation ($13,000). Subtracting these three excluded amounts ($28,000 + $9,000 + $13,000 = $50,000) from the $450,000 turnkey invoice yields a net Price Actually Paid or Payable (PAPP) of $400,000. Next, under § 152.103(b)(1)(i) and (iv), we add the packing costs incurred by the buyer ($6,500) and the patent royalty that the buyer is required to pay as a condition of the sale for exportation to the United States ($16,000). Calculation: $400,000 + $6,500 + $16,000 = $422,500.

distractors.A: $400,000 correctly deducts the $50,000 in post-importation exclusions ($450,000 - $28,000 - $9,000 - $13,000) but omits the mandatory statutory additions for export packing ($6,500) and the condition-of-sale royalty ($16,000).
distractors.B: $416,000 adds the $16,000 condition-of-sale royalty to $400,000 but forgets to add the $6,500 export packing costs incurred by the buyer under § 152.103(b)(1)(i).
distractors.C: CORRECT ($422,500): $450,000 - $28,000 (post-importation assembly) - $9,000 (U.S. inland freight) - $13,000 (U.S. duties) + $6,500 (buyer packing costs) + $16,000 (condition-of-sale royalty).
distractors.D: $450,500 fails to deduct the $28,000 post-importation erection/assembly charge ($422,500 + $28,000).
distractors.E: $472,500 fails to deduct any of the $50,000 in separately itemized post-importation charges and duties ($450,000 + $6,500 + $16,000).

questions.stem: An Ohio manufacturer imported 10,000 kg of designated wafers on June 1, 2024. Eligible duties and fees total $50,500. In January 2026 it uses domestic wafers of the same eight-digit classification in production and exports the unused finished goods to Germany in March 2026. The ceiling is $48,000; no percentage reduction applies.
The ceiling is $50,500 because fees count at 100%.

questions.goldenQuote: 99 percent of the lesser of

socraticHints: Compare both duty-and-fee bases.

questions.stem:
Meridian Retail Group imports two different packaged products in shrink-wrapped retail display boxes ready for direct sale to consumers without repacking:
• Product 1 ('Executive Commuter Gift Box'): Contains one ceramic insulated travel coffee mug (Heading 6912, value $8.00), one pair of knitted merino wool dress socks (Heading 6115, value $9.00), and one stainless-steel ballpoint pen (Heading 9608, value $7.50).
• Product 2 ('At-Home Pasta Dinner Kit'): Contains one box of uncooked dry durum wheat spaghetti (Heading 1902, value $3.20), one sealed pouch of tomato basil pasta sauce (Heading 2103, value $1.80), and one small packet of grated Parmesan cheese (Heading 0406, value $0.90).

Under the General Rules of Interpretation (GRI), how must Product 1 and Product 2 be classified?

options.text: Both Product 1 and Product 2 qualify as retail sets under GRI 3(b); Product 1 is classified entirely in Heading 6115 (highest value component), and Product 2 is classified entirely in Heading 1902.

Both Product 1 and Product 2 qualify as retail sets under GRI 3(b), but because no single component imparts essential character to Product 1, Product 1 is classified in Heading 9608 under GRI 3(c) (last in numerical order), while Product 2 is classified in Heading 1902.

Product 1 FAILS the GRI 3(b) retail set test because its articles are not put up together to meet a particular need or carry out a specific activity, so the mug (6912), socks (6115), and pen (9608) must each be classified separately; Product 2 QUALIFIES as a GRI 3(b) retail set and is classified as a single unit under Heading 1902 (the pasta component imparting essential character).
Neither Product 1 nor Product 2 qualifies as a retail set under GRI 3(b) because food items and consumer gift items must always be classified separately under GRI 1.
Product 1 is classified as a retail set under GRI 3(c) in Heading 9608, whereas each food item in Product 2 must be classified separately under Headings 1902, 2103, and 0406.

questions.targetCitation: HTSUS GRI 3(b) & Explanatory Note X (3-Prong Retail Set Test)
questions.goldenQuote: (2) Consist of products or articles put up together to meet a particular need or carry out a specific activity (Note: If a retail package contains disparate items that do NOT work together toward a single specific activity—for example, a promotional gift basket containing a ceramic coffee mug, a pair of cotton socks, and a ballpoint pen—it FAILS prong 2, is NOT a GRI 3(b) set, and EVERY item must be classified separately under its own HTSUS heading!); and
questions.shortestPathHint: HTSUS & GRI -> GRI 1–6 -> HTSUS GRI 3 (Rule 3(b) Retail Sets 3-Prong Test)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Before applying 'essential character' under GRI 3(b) or 'last in numerical order' under GRI 3(c), verify whether each retail package legally qualifies as 'goods put up in sets for retail sale'.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open HTSUS & GRI -> GRI 1–6 -> HTSUS GRI 3 and examine the Mandatory 3-Prong Test for retail sets under GRI 3(b).

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Check Prong 2 ('put up together to meet a particular need or carry out a specific activity'). Do a coffee mug, socks, and a pen work together to perform a single activity? No! Therefore Product 1 fails Prong 2 and each item classifies separately, whereas Product 2 (spaghetti, sauce, Parmesan) combines to prepare a pasta meal.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under HTSUS GRI 3(b) and Explanatory Note X, a package qualifies as 'goods put up in sets for retail sale' ONLY if it satisfies all three prongs: (1) at least two articles prima facie classifiable in different headings; (2) put up together to meet a particular need or carry out a specific activity; and (3) packaged for direct retail sale without repacking. Product 1 (a ceramic mug, wool socks, and a ballpoint pen) consists of disparate items that do not interact to carry out a specific activity (drinking coffee, dressing one's feet, and writing are unrelated activities). Because Product 1 fails Prong 2, it is NOT a GRI 3(b) set, and each item must be classified separately under GRI 1 (Headings 6912, 6115, and 9608). Conversely, Product 2 (spaghetti, pasta sauce, and grated Parmesan) satisfies all three prongs because the ingredients are used together to prepare a spaghetti meal, and the spaghetti (Heading 1902) imparts the essential character of the set under GRI 3(b).

distractors.A: Incorrect because Product 1 fails Prong 2 of the GRI 3(b) retail set definition; disparate gift items cannot be grouped under the highest-value item.
distractors.B: Incorrect because GRI 3(c) ('last in numerical order') applies to sets only AFTER a package first qualifies as a valid retail set under GRI 3(b). Since Product 1 fails the retail set test, GRI 3(c) cannot be invoked.
distractors.C: CORRECT: Product 1 fails Prong 2 (no unified specific activity) and is classified item-by-item, while Product 2 satisfies all three prongs of GRI 3(b) and is classified by its essential character (Heading 1902).
distractors.D: Incorrect because multi-ingredient meal kits whose components are prepared together into a single dish (like a pasta dinner kit) are classic examples of valid GRI 3(b) retail sets.
distractors.E: Incorrect because it reverses the legal outcome for both products.

questions.stem:
Symphony Imports LLC enters a single ocean container from Japan containing two commercial product lines:
• Line 1: 200 professional acoustic guitars (Heading 9202) and 250 hard-shell molded guitar cases specially shaped and fitted to hold the guitars and suitable for long-term use (200 of the cases contain the imported guitars, while the remaining 50 identical empty cases are packed in a separate carton as spare replacement cases for Symphony's retail store).
• Line 2: 80 heavy-duty seamless high-pressure steel gas cylinders (Heading 7311) imported filled with compressed argon gas (Heading 2804); the steel cylinders are equipped with refill valves and are designed to be returned, refilled, and circulated repeatedly for 15 years.

Under HTSUS General Rule of Interpretation 5 (GRI 5(a) and GRI 5(b)), how must the guitar cases and the steel gas cylinders be classified?

options.text: All 250 guitar cases are classified with the guitars under Heading 9202 pursuant to GRI 5(a), and all 80 steel cylinders are classified with the argon gas under Heading 2804 pursuant to GRI 5(b).

Only the 200 guitar cases entered with the 200 guitars are classified with the guitars under Heading 9202 pursuant to GRI 5(a), while the 50 excess spare guitar cases must be classified separately under Heading 4202; furthermore, the 80 heavy-duty reusable steel gas cylinders must be classified separately under Heading 7311 because GRI 5(b) is not binding on packing containers clearly suitable for repetitive use.

All 250 guitar cases must be classified separately under Heading 4202 because hard-shell cases are durable goods, while the 80 steel cylinders are classified with the argon gas under Heading 2804 pursuant to GRI 5(b).

Only the 200 guitar cases entered with the guitars are classified under Heading 9202 (with the 50 spare cases in Heading 4202), while the 80 steel cylinders are classified as argon gas under Heading 2804 because all containers entered with goods classify with their contents under GRI 5(b).
Both the guitars with cases and the cylinders with argon gas are classified under Heading 9202 and Heading 7311 respectively by application of GRI 3(c) (last in numerical order).

questions.goldenQuote: (b) Packing Materials and Packing Containers: Subject to the provisions of Rule 5(a) above, packing materials and packing containers entered with the goods therein shall be classified with the goods if they are of a kind normally used for packing such goods. However, this provision is not binding when such packing materials or packing containers are clearly suitable for repetitive use.
questions.shortestPathHint: HTSUS & GRI -> GRI 1–6 -> HTSUS GRI 5 (Rule 5(a) Fitted Camera/Instrument Cases & Rule 5(b) Packing Containers)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): GRI 5 governs special containers and packing materials, but both Rule 5(a) and Rule 5(b) contain critical exceptions tested heavily on the CBLE.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open HTSUS & GRI -> GRI 1–6 -> HTSUS GRI 5 and inspect the 'Crucial Exam Traps' under both Rule 5(a) and Rule 5(b).

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Under GRI 5(a), fitted musical instrument cases classify with the instruments ONLY to the extent they are matched 1-to-1 with the entered instruments (200 cases in 9202; 50 excess cases in 4202). Under GRI 5(b), packing containers 'clearly suitable for repetitive use' (like heavy-duty refillable steel gas cylinders) are excluded from classifying with their contents and classify separately in Heading 7311!

explanation.correctReasoning: Under HTSUS GRI 5(a), musical instrument cases that are specially shaped or fitted, suitable for long-term use, and entered with the articles for which they are intended are classified with those articles (Heading 9202). However, the 50 extra guitar cases imported in excess of the 200 guitars are not 'entered with the articles for which they are intended' on a 1-to-1 basis and must be classified separately on their own merits under Heading 4202. Under HTSUS GRI 5(b), ordinary packing containers entered with goods are classified with the goods, EXCEPT that 'this provision is not binding when such packing materials or packing containers are clearly suitable for repetitive use.' Heavy-duty seamless steel compressed-gas cylinders designed for 15 years of continuous refilling and return circulation are the classic example of repetitive-use containers and must be classified separately under Heading 7311 rather than with the argon gas (Heading 2804).

distractors.A: Erroneously classifies the 50 excess spare guitar cases under GRI 5(a) and ignores the repetitive-use exception in GRI 5(b) for the refillable steel cylinders.
distractors.B: CORRECT: Applies both the 1-to-1 matching requirement of GRI 5(a) (200 cases in 9202; 50 excess cases in 4202) and the repetitive-use exception of GRI 5(b) (80 refillable steel cylinders in 7311).
distractors.C: Erroneously rejects GRI 5(a) for the 200 fitted cases entered with the guitars and ignores the GRI 5(b) repetitive-use exception for the steel cylinders.
distractors.D: Correctly splits the 200 vs. 50 guitar cases under GRI 5(a), but fails to apply the GRI 5(b) exception for packing containers clearly suitable for repetitive use.
distractors.E: GRI 3(c) does not apply to containers and packing materials governed specifically by GRI 5(a) and GRI 5(b).

questions.stem: Velocity Cycling Inc. imports a single container shipment from Taiwan containing knocked-down bicycle assembly kits. Specifically, the shipment consists of 500 aluminum bicycle frames, 500 front forks, 500 handlebars, 500 cranksets/drivetrains, and 1,100 complete bicycle wheels (each bicycle requires 1 frame, 1 fork, 1 handlebar, 1 drivetrain, and 2 wheels; bicycle saddles/seats are omitted and will be sourced domestically in the United States after importation). Under HTSUS General Rule of Interpretation 2(a) (GRI 2(a)), how must this shipment be classified?

options.text: Every component must be classified separately as bicycle parts under Heading 8714 because the articles are imported unassembled and lack bicycle saddles.
The entire shipment—including all 1,100 wheels—is classified as 500 complete bicycles under Heading 8712 pursuant to GRI 2(a).

Under GRI 2(a), the 500 matched sets of frames, forks, handlebars, drivetrains, and 1,000 wheels (2 wheels per bicycle) are classified as 500 complete bicycles under Heading 8712 because, as entered in unassembled condition, they have the essential character of complete bicycles despite lacking saddles; however, the 100 excess wheels beyond the exact count needed to assemble the 500 bicycles must be classified separately as bicycle parts under Heading 8714.
The shipment is classified under Heading 8714 pursuant to GRI 3(c) (last in numerical order between Heading 8712 and Heading 8714).
The shipment is classified as raw aluminum articles of Chapter 76 under GRI 1 until assembled in a U.S. bonded warehouse.

questions.goldenQuote: 2. (a) Any reference in a heading to an article shall be taken to include a reference to that article incomplete or unfinished, provided that, as entered, the incomplete or unfinished article has the essential character of the complete or finished article. It shall also include a reference to that article complete or finished (or falling to be classified as complete or finished by virtue of this rule), entered unassembled or disassembled.
questions.shortestPathHint: HTSUS & GRI -> GRI 1–6 -> HTSUS GRI 2 (Rule 2(a) Incomplete/Unfinished/Unassembled Articles)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): GRI 2(a) has two prongs: (1) incomplete or unfinished articles having the essential character of the complete article, and (2) articles entered unassembled or disassembled.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open HTSUS & GRI -> GRI 1–6 -> HTSUS GRI 2 and read Rule 2(a) together with the CBP Legal Interpretation Notes on 'Unassembled or Disassembled' goods.

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Check how many wheels are needed for 500 bicycles (500 x 2 = 1,000 wheels). The 500 unassembled kits (with 1,000 wheels) have the essential character of complete bicycles (Heading 8712) under GRI 2(a) even without seats, while the 100 excess wheels must be classified separately as bicycle parts (Heading 8714)!

explanation.correctReasoning: Under HTSUS GRI 2(a), any reference in a heading to an article includes that article incomplete or unfinished, provided that as entered it has the essential character of the complete or finished article, and also includes complete or finished articles (or articles falling to be classified as complete or finished by virtue of GRI 2(a)) entered unassembled or disassembled. A bicycle consisting of a frame, fork, handlebars, drivetrain, and two wheels clearly possesses the essential character of a complete bicycle of Heading 8712 even without a saddle. However, under GRI 2(a) and its Explanatory Notes, excess components beyond the exact number required to assemble the 500 bicycles—here, the 100 extra wheels (1,100 imported minus 1,000 required for 500 bicycles)—cannot be included with the complete bicycles and must be classified separately on their own merits as bicycle parts under Heading 8714.

distractors.A: Incorrect because GRI 2(a) expressly classifies unassembled and incomplete articles having the essential character of the finished good under the heading for the complete article (Heading 8712).
distractors.B: Incorrect because excess parts imported beyond the exact count needed to assemble the complete units (the 100 extra wheels) must be classified separately in Heading 8714.
distractors.C: CORRECT: Applies both prongs of GRI 2(a) to classify the 500 unassembled kits (using 1,000 wheels) as bicycles in Heading 8712 and separates the 100 surplus wheels into Heading 8714.
distractors.D: Incorrect because a heading for a complete article (8712) and its parts heading (8714) are resolved via GRI 1 and GRI 2(a), never GRI 3(c).
distractors.E: Incorrect because manufactured bicycle components are articles of Chapter 87, not raw aluminum of Chapter 76.

options.text: Items 1, 2, and 3 are all classified in Heading 8471 as automatic data processing machines and units thereof, and Item 4 is classified in Heading 8431 as a part of a conveyor machine.

Item 1 is classified in Heading 8471 (ADP machines); Item 2 is classified in Heading 8517 (telecommunications apparatus, excluded from 8471 by Chapter 84 Note 6(D)/(E)); Item 3 is classified in Heading 8528 (monitors, excluded from 8471 by Chapter 84 Note 6(D)/(E)); and Item 4 is classified in Heading 8501 (electric motors) because under Section XVI Note 2(a), parts which are goods included in any of the headings of Chapter 84 or 85 are in all cases classified in their respective headings.

Item 1 is classified in Heading 8471; Item 2 is classified in Heading 8517; Item 3 is classified in Heading 8528; and Item 4 is classified in Heading 8428 (with the conveyor machine) under Section XVI Note 2(b).
Item 1 and Item 3 are classified in Heading 8471; Item 2 is classified in Heading 8517; and Item 4 is classified in Heading 8503 (parts of electric motors).
All four items are classified in Heading 8543 as electrical machines and apparatus having individual functions not specified elsewhere.

questions.targetCitation: HTSUS Section XVI Note 2(a) & Chapter 84 Note 6 (Headings 8471, 8517, 8528, 8501)
questions.goldenQuote: (a) Parts which are goods included in any of the headings of Chapter 84 or 85 (other than headings 8409, 8431, 8448, 8466, 8473, 8487, 8503, 8522, 8529, 8538 and 8548) are in all cases to be classified in their respective headings (e.g., an electric motor designed solely for a washing machine is still classified in Heading 8501 as an electric motor under Note 2(a), NOT in Heading 8450 as a washing machine part!);
questions.shortestPathHint: HTSUS & GRI -> Chapters 84, 85 & 95 -> HTSUS Section XVI Notes & Headings 8471 / 8517 / 8528
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Under GRI 1, Section XVI Note 2 governs machine parts across Chapters 84 and 85, while Chapter 84 Note 6 defines the boundary between ADP machines (8471), telecom apparatus (8517), and monitors (8528).
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open HTSUS & GRI -> Chapters 84, 85 & 95 -> HTSUS Section XVI Notes & Headings 8471 / 8517 / 8528.

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Check Section XVI Note 2(a) first before Note 2(b)! Because an electric motor is itself a named good of Heading 8501, Note 2(a) forces it into Heading 8501 even if custom-bracketed solely for another machine. And under Chapter 84 Note 6(D)/(E), smartphones/routers classify in 8517 and monitors classify in 8528.

explanation.correctReasoning: Applying GRI 1 together with the Section XVI and Chapter 84 Legal Notes: (1) Item 1 (laptops) satisfies Chapter 84 Note 6(A) as an automatic data processing (ADP) machine under Heading 8471; (2) Item 2 (smartphones and Wi-Fi routers) is excluded from Heading 8471 by Chapter 84 Note 6(D)/(E) because its principal function is data/voice transmission and reception, placing it in Heading 8517; (3) Item 3 (27-inch LCD computer monitors) is excluded from Heading 8471 by Chapter 84 Note 6(D)/(E) and classified in Heading 8528 (specifically 8528.52.00); and (4) Item 4 (an electric motor designed solely for a conveyor machine) is governed by Section XVI Note 2(a), which mandates that parts which are themselves goods included in any heading of Chapter 84 or 85 (other than general parts headings) must IN ALL CASES be classified in their respective headings (Heading 8501 for electric motors)—you never reach Note 2(b)!

distractors.A: Fails to apply Chapter 84 Note 6(D)/(E) exclusions for telecom apparatus (8517) and monitors (8528) and skips Section XVI Note 2(a) for the electric motor.
distractors.B: CORRECT: 8471 for laptops, 8517 for smartphones/routers, 8528 for monitors, and 8501 for the electric motor pursuant to Section XVI Note 2(a).
distractors.C: Correctly classifies Items 1, 2, and 3, but falls into the classic CBLE trap of applying Section XVI Note 2(b) ('solely or principally used with a machine') before checking Note 2(a) ('goods included in any heading of Chapter 84 or 85').
distractors.D: Erroneously places computer monitors in Heading 8471 (contrary to Chapter 84 Note 6) and classifies a complete electric motor as a motor part in Heading 8503.
distractors.E: Heading 8543 is a residual basket heading that applies only when machines are not specified or included elsewhere in Chapter 84 or 85.

questions.stem: An entry specialist is classifying a specialized industrial liquid pump that has already been properly placed into 4-digit Heading 8413 pursuant to GRI 1. Inside Heading 8413, the tariff schedule contains several one-dash ('-') subheadings, each subdivided into multiple two-dash ('--') and three-dash ('---') subheadings. The entry specialist notices a two-dash ('--') subheading nested under a lower one-dash ('-') residual branch that appears to mention the pump's operating pressure, and wants to jump directly to that two-dash subheading without first comparing the competing one-dash ('-') subheadings at the top level. Under HTSUS General Rule of Interpretation 6 (GRI 6), what is the binding legal rule governing subheading comparisons within a 4-digit heading?

options.text: A classifier may jump directly to any 8-digit or 10-digit subheading anywhere within a 4-digit heading regardless of indent/dash level whenever the lower subheading has a lower duty rate.

For legal purposes, classification in the subheadings of a heading is determined according to the terms of those subheadings and any related subheading notes (and, mutatis mutandis, GRIs 1 through 5), on the strict understanding that ONLY subheadings at the same level (same dash/indent level) are comparable—meaning the classifier must first compare and select the proper one-dash ('-') subheading before comparing the two-dash ('--') subheadings nested underneath it.
Section and Chapter Notes cease to apply once a classifier moves from the 4-digit heading level to the 6-digit or 8-digit subheading level under GRI 6.
Under GRI 6, all subheading disputes within a 4-digit heading are automatically resolved by choosing the subheading that appears first in numerical order.
GRI 6 applies only when comparing two different 4-digit headings across two different chapters of the HTSUS.

questions.goldenQuote: 6. For legal purposes, the classification of goods in the subheadings of a heading shall be determined according to the terms of those subheadings and any related subheading notes and, mutatis mutandis, to the above rules, on the understanding that only subheadings at the same level are comparable.
questions.shortestPathHint: HTSUS & GRI -> GRI 1–6 -> HTSUS GRI 6 (Rule 6 — Subheading Comparison at the Same Dash Level)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Once the 4-digit heading is fixed under GRIs 1–4, how do you navigate the indented 6-digit and 8-digit subheadings underneath that heading?
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open HTSUS & GRI -> GRI 1–6 -> HTSUS GRI 6 and read the statutory rule and the CBP Legal Interpretation Note on GRI 6.

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Under GRI 6, ONLY subheadings at the same dash/indent level are comparable! You must compare one-dash ('-') against one-dash ('-') first, lock in the winning one-dash branch, and only then compare the two-dash ('--') subheadings nested beneath that branch.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under HTSUS General Rule of Interpretation 6 (GRI 6), for legal purposes, the classification of goods in the subheadings of a 4-digit heading shall be determined according to the terms of those subheadings and any related subheading notes and, mutatis mutandis, to GRIs 1 through 5, on the strict understanding that ONLY subheadings at the same level (i.e., the same indentation/dash level) are comparable. For the purposes of GRI 6, the relative Section, Chapter, and Subchapter Notes also apply unless the context otherwise requires. Therefore, a classifier must first compare only the one-dash ('-') subheadings within the 4-digit heading and select the governing one-dash subheading before proceeding to compare the two-dash ('--') subheadings nested underneath it.

distractors.A: Violates GRI 6's core mandate that only subheadings at the same indentation/dash level are comparable.
distractors.B: CORRECT: Accurately states the GRI 6 rule that subheadings are compared strictly at the same dash/indent level (one-dash vs. one-dash, then two-dash vs. two-dash) using the terms of the subheadings, Subheading Notes, and Section/Chapter Notes.
distractors.C: Directly contradicts the second sentence of GRI 6, which states that 'the relative section, chapter and subchapter notes also apply, unless the context otherwise requires.'
distractors.D: Incorrect because GRIs 1 through 5 apply mutatis mutandis at each dash level, and ifGRI 3(c) is reached, it selects the subheading occurring LAST (not first) in numerical order at that same dash level.
distractors.E: GRI 6 governs 6-digit/8-digit subheading classification WITHIN a single 4-digit heading; 4-digit headings are determined using GRIs 1 through 4.

options.text: All four items are classified as toys or festive articles in Chapter 95 (Heading 9503 or 9505) because they are marketed and sold exclusively for children's play and amusement.

Under GRI 1 and Chapter 95 Note 1: Item 1 is excluded from Chapter 95 by Note 1(v) as utilitarian kitchenware and classified by constituent material in Heading 7323 (stainless steel kitchen articles); Item 2 is excluded from Chapter 95 by Note 1(e) ('Fancy dress of textiles, of chapter 61 or 62') and classified as woven wearing apparel in Chapter 62; Item 3 is excluded from Chapter 95 by Note 1(d) and classified in Heading 4202; and ONLY Item 4 is classified as a toy in Heading 9503.00.00.
Items 1 and 4 are classified in Heading 9503.00.00 as toys, while Item 2 is classified in Heading 9505 as a festive carnival article and Item 3 is classified in Heading 4202.
Item 1 is classified in Heading 7323, but Items 2, 3, and 4 are all classified in Heading 9503.00.00 pursuant to GRI 3(b).
All four items are classified in Chapter 62 as children's textile accessories under GRI 3(c).

questions.goldenQuote: (v) Tableware, kitchenware, toilet articles, carpets and other textile floor coverings, apparel, bed linen, table linen, toilet linen, kitchen linen and similar articles having a utilitarian function (classified according to their constituent material).
questions.shortestPathHint: HTSUS & GRI -> Chapters 84, 85 & 95 -> HTSUS Chapter 95 Note 1 & Heading 9503
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Under GRI 1, you must check Chapter 95 Note 1 exclusions FIRST before classifying any children's product as a toy in Heading 9503.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open HTSUS & GRI -> Chapters 84, 85 & 95 -> HTSUS Chapter 95 Note 1 & Heading 9503.

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Check the three Chapter 95 Note 1 exclusions: Note 1(v) excludes kitchenware/tableware having a real utilitarian function (Item 1 -> Heading 7323 stainless steel kitchenware); Note 1(e) excludes durable textile fancy dress costumes (Item 2 -> Chapter 62 woven apparel); Note 1(d) excludes sports/toy bags of Heading 4202 (Item 3 -> Heading 4202). Only Item 4 (pretend plastic oven designed solely for amusement) classifies in Heading 9503.00.00!

explanation.correctReasoning: Under HTSUS GRI 1, classification is determined legally according to the terms of the headings and any relative Section or Chapter Notes. Chapter 95 Note 1 sets forth mandatory legal exclusions from Chapter 95: (1) Under Chapter 95 Note 1(v), tableware, kitchenware, and similar articles having a utilitarian function are excluded from Chapter 95 and classified according to their constituent material—because Item 1 consists of real stainless-steel bakeware used to bake real food in an oven, it is utilitarian kitchenware of Heading 7323 even though sized and marketed for children; (2) Under Chapter 95 Note 1(e), 'Fancy dress of textiles, of chapter 61 or 62' is excluded from Chapter 95, placing Item 2 (a durable woven textile costume) in Chapter 62; (3) Under Chapter 95 Note 1(d), sports bags and other containers of Heading 4202 are excluded from Chapter 95, placing Item 3 in Heading 4202; and (4) Item 4 (a miniature non-heating plastic pretend play oven) satisfies the 'principal use for amusement' test and is classified as a toy in Heading 9503.00.00.

distractors.A: Ignores the binding legal exclusions in Chapter 95 Note 1(d), 1(e), and 1(v); marketing to children does not override Chapter 95 Legal Notes under GRI 1.
distractors.B: CORRECT: Applies Chapter 95 Note 1(v) (Item 1 -> 7323), Note 1(e) (Item 2 -> Ch. 62), Note 1(d) (Item 3 -> 4202), and Heading 9503.00.00 (Item 4).
distractors.C: Fails to apply Note 1(v) to the functional stainless-steel bakeware (Item 1) and Note 1(e) to the durable woven textile costume (Item 2).
distractors.D: Fails to apply Note 1(e) to the textile costume and Note 1(d) to the Heading 4202 bag.
distractors.E: Incorrect because stainless-steel cookware, nylon bags, and plastic toys are not articles of Chapter 62.

questions.category: IRS SEE Part 3 — Circular 230 (31 CFR Part 10)
questions.stem: [IRS Enrolled Agent Track — SEE Part 3] During an IRS examination of client Horizon Logistics Inc., an IRS Revenue Agent makes a proper and lawful written request to Enrolled Agent Thomas Greene for Horizon's warehouse inventory ledgers from two years ago. Greene does not have the inventory ledgers in his possession, and Horizon's current president informs Greene that the ledgers were retained by Horizon's former outside bookkeeper, Carla Moss, after her contract ended. None of the records are legally privileged. Under Treasury Department Circular 230 (31 CFR § 10.20), what are Enrolled Agent Greene's exact obligations regarding the Revenue Agent's request?

options.text: Greene must hire a private investigator to independently verify whether Carla Moss actually possesses the ledgers and subpoena Carla Moss before responding to the IRS.

Greene must promptly notify the requesting IRS officer that neither he nor his client possesses the records, provide any information Greene has regarding the identity of the person (Carla Moss) whom he believes may have possession or control of the requested records, and make reasonable inquiry of his client regarding the identity of any person who may have possession or control, without being required to make inquiry of any other person or independently verify the client's information.
Greene may refuse to respond to the IRS request entirely because the Enrollee-Client privilege under Circular 230 permanently shields all accounting ledgers from IRS examination.
Greene must reconstruct the missing inventory ledgers from memory and submit estimated figures to the IRS without disclosing that the original ledgers are held by Carla Moss.
Greene must immediately withdraw from representing Horizon Logistics Inc. whenever a requested document is not in the practitioner's physical office.

questions.goldenQuote: reasonable inquiry of his or her client
questions.shortestPathHint: 31 CFR Part 10 -> Subpart B -> § 10.20 (Information to be furnished)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Check what Circular 230 requires when the IRS makes a proper and lawful request for non-privileged records that are not in the possession or control of the practitioner or client.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 31 CFR Part 10 -> Subpart B -> § 10.20 and read paragraph (a)(2).

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Under § 10.20(a)(2), the practitioner must promptly notify the IRS officer, provide any information regarding who may have possession/control, and make reasonable inquiry OF THE CLIENT—but is explicitly NOT required to make inquiry of any other person or independently verify the client's statement!

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 31 CFR § 10.20(a)(1), a practitioner must promptly submit records or information upon a proper and lawful request by an IRS officer unless the practitioner believes in good faith and on reasonable grounds that the records are privileged. Under § 10.20(a)(2), where the requested records are not in the possession or control of the practitioner or the client, the practitioner must: (1) promptly notify the requesting IRS officer; (2) provide any information the practitioner has regarding the identity of any person believed to have possession or control of the records; and (3) make reasonable inquiry of the client regarding the identity of any person who may have possession or control. However, § 10.20(a)(2) expressly states that the practitioner is NOT required to make inquiry of any other person or independently verify the information provided by the client regarding the identity of such persons.

distractors.A: Directly contradicts 31 CFR § 10.20(a)(2), which states that the practitioner is not required to make inquiry of any third person or independently verify the client's information.
distractors.B: CORRECT: Tracks the exact statutory and regulatory text of 31 CFR § 10.20(a)(1)–(2).
distractors.C: Ordinary accounting and inventory ledgers are not privileged, and withholding non-privileged information without a good-faith reasonable belief of privilege violates § 10.20(a)(1).
distractors.D: Submitting fabricated or undisclosed reconstructions violates due diligence under § 10.22 and § 10.20.
distractors.E: Lack of possession of a third-party record does not require or justify withdrawal from representation.

questions.stem: [IRS Enrolled Agent Track — SEE Part 3] Enrolled Agent Sarah Jenkins is retained by a new business client, Oakridge Landscaping LLC, to prepare its current-year federal income tax return. While reviewing the prior year's tax return (which was prepared by a different accountant) alongside Oakridge's general ledger, Jenkins discovers that the client omitted $140,000 of taxable cash landscaping receipts from the prior year's Schedule C. Under Treasury Department Circular 230 (31 CFR § 10.21), what are Jenkins' exact legal obligations upon discovering the client's prior-year omission?

options.text: Promptly notify the IRS Criminal Investigation Division in writing of the $140,000 omission and transmit copies of the client's general ledger to the IRS.
Prepare and electronically file an amended Form 1040-X for the prior year on the client's behalf immediately, even if the client refuses to sign or authorize the amended return.

Promptly advise the client of the fact of the noncompliance, error, or omission, AND advise the client of the consequences as provided under the Internal Revenue Code and regulations of such noncompliance, error, or omission (without unilaterally notifying the IRS).
Ignore the prior-year omission completely because Jenkins did not sign or prepare the prior year's tax return.
Automatically report the prior tax preparer to the Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) within 15 calendar days and impound the client's accounting records.

questions.goldenQuote: advise the client promptly of the fact of such noncompliance, error, or omission
questions.shortestPathHint: 31 CFR Part 10 -> Subpart B -> § 10.21 (Knowledge of client's omission)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Compare how IRS Circular 230 handles a client's tax omission with how 19 CFR § 111.32 handles a customs client's error.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Switch to the '31 CFR Part 10' corpus tab -> Subpart B -> § 10.21 ('Knowledge of client's omission').

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Under 31 CFR § 10.21, the practitioner must promptly advise the client of (1) the fact of the error/omission AND (2) the consequences under the Internal Revenue Code and regulations. The practitioner is NEVER allowed to report the client's omission to the IRS unilaterally or file an amended return without client consent!

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 31 CFR § 10.21 (Circular 230), a practitioner who knows that a client has not complied with the U.S. revenue laws or has made an error in or omission from any return or document submitted under the revenue laws (regardless of who prepared the prior return) has two mandatory duties: (1) promptly advise the client of the fact of such noncompliance, error, or omission; and (2) advise the client of the consequences under the Internal Revenue Code and regulations (such as accuracy-related penalties, interest, and statute of limitations implications). Circular 230 does NOT authorize the practitioner to inform the IRS without client consent, nor can a practitioner file an amended return without the taxpayer's authorization.

distractors.A: Unilaterally disclosing confidential client tax information to the IRS without a lawful summons or client consent violates IRC § 7216 and is not permitted by Circular 230 § 10.21.
distractors.B: A practitioner cannot file an amended tax return (Form 1040-X) without the client's signature and authorization.
distractors.C: CORRECT: Accurately states the two mandatory practitioner obligations under 31 CFR § 10.21.
distractors.D: 31 CFR § 10.21 applies whenever a retained practitioner discovers a client's error or omission on any submitted return, even if another preparer signed the prior-year return.
distractors.E: Circular 230 § 10.21 does not mandate reporting the prior preparer within 15 days or impounding client records (in fact, § 10.28 requires returning client records promptly upon request).

questions.category: IRS SEE Part 3 — Circular 230 (31 CFR Part 10)
questions.stem: [IRS Enrolled Agent Track — SEE Part 3] Enrolled Agent Elena Brooks manages a busy tax practice and delegates the depreciation schedule calculations for a commercial real estate client's Form 1065 partnership return to a junior staff accountant in her firm, resulting in an inadvertent computational misstatement on the return submitted to the IRS. Under 31 CFR § 10.22(a) and (b), in what three areas must a practitioner exercise due diligence, and under what exact circumstances will Brooks be presumed to have exercised due diligence when relying on the work product of another person?

options.text: A practitioner is strictly and unconditionally liable under Circular 230 for every arithmetic error made by an employee or specialist, and reliance on another person's work product is never permitted.

A practitioner must exercise due diligence in (1) preparing/assisting in preparing, approving, and filing tax returns and IRS documents, (2) determining the correctness of oral or written representations made to the Department of the Treasury, and (3) determining the correctness of oral or written representations made to clients regarding IRS matters; furthermore, the practitioner will be presumed to have exercised due diligence when relying on the work product of another person if the practitioner used reasonable care in engaging, supervising, training, and evaluating the person, taking proper account of the nature of the relationship.

A practitioner is only required to exercise due diligence on written representations made under oath to an IRS Appeals Officer, and has no due diligence obligation regarding oral advice given to clients.
A practitioner is automatically presumed to have exercised due diligence whenever work is delegated to another person, even if the practitioner provided zero training, supervision, or evaluation.
A practitioner may rely on the work product of another person only if that other person is a licensed attorney or Certified Public Accountant who co-signs Form 2848.

questions.goldenQuote: reasonable care in engaging, supervising, training, and evaluating the person
questions.shortestPathHint: 31 CFR Part 10 -> Subpart B -> § 10.22 (Diligence as to accuracy)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Check the general rule of due diligence in Circular 230 and the specific safe-harbor presumption for relying on the work product of others.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 31 CFR Part 10 -> Subpart B -> § 10.22 and read paragraphs (a)(1)–(3) and (b).

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Notice that § 10.22(a) covers BOTH oral and written representations to the Treasury AND to clients, and § 10.22(b) creates a presumption of due diligence if the practitioner used reasonable care in engaging, supervising, training, and evaluating the other person.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 31 CFR § 10.22(a), a practitioner must exercise due diligence in three domains: (1) preparing or assisting in the preparation of, approving, and filing tax returns, documents, affidavits, and other papers relating to IRS matters; (2) determining the correctness of oral or written representations made by the practitioner to the Department of the Treasury; and (3) determining the correctness of oral or written representations made by the practitioner to clients with reference to any matter administered by the IRS. Under § 10.22(b), a practitioner will be presumed to have exercised due diligence when relying on the work product of another person provided the practitioner used reasonable care in engaging, supervising, training, and evaluating that person, taking proper account of the nature of the relationship between the practitioner and the person.

distractors.A: Incorrect because 31 CFR § 10.22(b) explicitly provides a due diligence presumption when a practitioner reasonably engages, supervises, trains, and evaluates the person whose work product is relied upon.
distractors.B: CORRECT: Accurately sets forth the three due diligence domains of § 10.22(a) and the four-factor reasonable-care standard for relying on others under § 10.22(b).
distractors.C: Incorrect because § 10.22(a)(2) and (3) explicitly apply to both oral AND written representations made to the Treasury and to clients.
distractors.D: Incorrect because blind delegation without reasonable care in engaging, supervising, training, and evaluating the person forfeits the § 10.22(b) safe harbor.
distractors.E: Incorrect because § 10.22(b) applies to reliance on the work product of 'another person' (including staff accountants or appraisers) when reasonable care is used, not solely co-signing attorneys or CPAs.

questions.category: IRS SEE Part 3 — Circular 230 (31 CFR Part 10)
questions.stem: An enrolled agent proposes a contingent fee for each independent engagement in the 2025 exam reference year. A is administrative collection representation to negotiate an installment agreement, with no examination, written challenge, refund claim or judicial proceeding. B is representation during an IRS examination of an original corporate return. C is a refund claim solely about assessed statutory interest and penalties. Which arrangements fall within the express contingent-fee exceptions in § 10.27(b)?

options.text: None.
A, B and C if the clients agree in writing.
B and C.
A only.
C only.

questions.goldenQuote: the determination of statutory interest or penalties
questions.shortestPathHint: Read § 10.27(b)(1)–(4) in the 2025 edition.
socraticHints: Separate collection representation from an examination.
Read § 10.27(b)(1)–(4) in the 2025 edition.
For C, identify the sole subject of the refund claim.

explanation.correctReasoning: The examination in B fits paragraph (b)(2)(i), and C fits (b)(3). The routine collection representation in A fits none of (b)(2)–(4).

distractors.A: The regulation lists both the examination and interest-or-penalty exceptions.
distractors.B: Client consent cannot create an exception.
distractors.C: The examination in B fits paragraph (b)(2)(i), and C fits (b)(3). The routine collection representation in A fits none of (b)(2)–(4).
distractors.D: A is outside the exceptions and B and C are inside them.
distractors.E: B also fits an express exception.

questions.category: IRS SEE Part 3 — Circular 230 (31 CFR Part 10)
questions.stem: [IRS Enrolled Agent Track — SEE Part 3] Enrolled Agent Diana Cho is asked to represent two former business partners, Alex and Jordan, in an IRS audit concerning the allocation of partnership losses between them—a matter in which Alex's tax position is directly adverse to Jordan's tax position. Cho reasonably believes that she can provide competent and diligent representation to both Alex and Jordan, and the dual representation is not prohibited by law. Both Alex and Jordan orally agree to waive the conflict of interest during a meeting on June 1. Under Treasury Department Circular 230 (31 CFR § 10.29), what written confirmation deadline and record-retention period must Cho satisfy to represent both clients legally?

options.text: Oral informed consent witnessed by a notary public is sufficient under Circular 230, and no written confirmation or retention period is required.

Each affected client must waive the conflict of interest and give informed consent, confirmed in writing by each affected client within a reasonable period after the informed consent, but in no event later than 30 days; furthermore, copies of the written consents must be retained by the practitioner for at least 36 months from the date of the conclusion of the representation of the affected clients.
Written confirmation of informed consent must be signed by the IRS Revenue Agent within 60 days, and the practitioner must retain the consent for 12 months from the date the conflict was discovered.
A conflict of interest involving direct adversity between two taxpayers before the IRS can never be waived under any circumstances, even with written consent.
Each affected client must confirm informed consent in writing within 90 days, and the practitioner must retain the written consents for 5 years from the filing of the partnership return.

questions.goldenQuote: but in no event later than 30 days
questions.shortestPathHint: 31 CFR Part 10 -> Subpart B -> § 10.29 (Conflicting interests)
socraticHints: Hint 1 (Concept): Check the exact conditions under which a practitioner may represent clients despite a conflict of interest, focusing on the two numeric timeframes in § 10.29.
Hint 2 (Navigation): Open 31 CFR Part 10 -> Subpart B -> § 10.29 and read paragraphs (b)(3) and (c).

Hint 3 (Trap Check): Memorize the 30-day / 36-month pair in § 10.29: informed consent must be confirmed in writing by EACH affected client within at most 30 days, and the practitioner must retain copies of the written consents for at least 36 months from the date of the CONCLUSION of the representation!

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 31 CFR § 10.29(a) and (b), when a conflict of interest exists, a practitioner may represent the affected clients ONLY if three cumulative conditions are met: (1) the practitioner reasonably believes they can provide competent and diligent representation to each affected client; (2) the representation is not prohibited by law; and (3) each affected client waives the conflict and gives informed consent, confirmed in writing by each affected client at the time the conflict is known (with the written confirmation made within a reasonable period after the informed consent, but in no event later than 30 days). Furthermore, under § 10.29(c), copies of the written consents must be retained by the practitioner for at least 36 months from the date of the conclusion of the representation of the affected clients and provided to any IRS officer or employee upon request.

distractors.A: Incorrect because § 10.29(b)(3) strictly requires informed consent to be confirmed in writing by each affected client within 30 days.
distractors.B: CORRECT: States the exact 30-day maximum window for written confirmation by each affected client (§ 10.29(b)(3)) and the 36-month retention period after conclusion of the representation (§ 10.29(c)).
distractors.C: Incorrect because the written consent is signed by each affected client (not the IRS Revenue Agent) within 30 days (not 60 days) and retained for 36 months after conclusion of the representation (not 12 months).
distractors.D: Incorrect because § 10.29(b) explicitly permits waiving a conflict of interest when all three conditions in (b)(1)–(3) are satisfied.
distractors.E: Incorrect because the written confirmation deadline is 30 days (not 90 days) and the retention period is 36 months (3 years) from the conclusion of the representation.

questions.category: IRS SEE Part 3 — Circular 230 (31 CFR Part 10)
questions.stem: A signing preparer evaluates an ordinary deduction for a 2025 return. It involves neither a tax shelter nor a reportable transaction. Supporting authorities establish reasonable basis but fall short of substantial authority. The client also supplies a travel summary that conflicts with bank statements. Which course fits the preparer standards?

options.text: Sign without disclosure because any nonfrivolous position suffices.

For the deduction use the applicable adequate-disclosure procedure for a reasonable-basis position. Advise the client about relevant penalties and opportunities for disclosure. Make reasonable inquiries to resolve the inconsistent travel information before relying on it.
Use a numerical probability as the only test and disregard disclosure.
Obtain a client waiver and ignore the conflicting statements.
Treat every item as requiring more-likely-than-not support and automatically report the client.

questions.goldenQuote: must make reasonable inquiries if the information as furnished appears to be incorrect
socraticHints: Identify the kind of position and the level of authority.
Assess the inconsistency independently of the position-disclosure question.

explanation.correctReasoning: For this ordinary position the facts establish reasonable basis and insufficient substantial authority. Consider the appropriate preparer disclosure steps under § 1.6694-2(d). Circular 230 also requires penalty advice where applicable and reasonable inquiry into an apparent inconsistency.

distractors.A: A merely nonfrivolous position does not meet the stated preparer standard.
distractors.B: For this ordinary position the facts establish reasonable basis and insufficient substantial authority. Consider the appropriate preparer disclosure steps under § 1.6694-2(d). Circular 230 also requires penalty advice where applicable and reasonable inquiry into an apparent inconsistency.
distractors.C: The regulations define legal standards and weigh authorities; this exercise assigns no percentage cutoff.
distractors.D: A private waiver cannot replace inquiry or the applicable disclosure procedure.
distractors.E: The ordinary position in this question has a different standard. These facts call for inquiry.
