questions.stem:
Maya is unmarried at year-end and lives alone in a rental apartment in Seattle. Her widowed mother lives independently in a separate assisted-living apartment in Portland. During the entire tax year, Maya pays 70% of the cost of maintaining her mother’s apartment and properly claims her mother as a qualifying relative dependent. Maya has no other dependents.

Under IRC § 2(b) and 26 CFR § 1.2-2, what is the most advantageous filing status Maya may claim?

options.text: Single, because a qualifying person must live in the taxpayer’s own home for more than half the year to claim Head of Household.

Head of Household, because a dependent parent does not have to live in the taxpayer’s own home when the taxpayer pays more than half the cost of maintaining the parent’s separate household for the entire year.
Qualifying Surviving Spouse, because Maya supports a widowed parent.
Head of Household only if Maya’s mother lives with Maya for at least 6 months during the calendar year.
Married Filing Separately, because supporting a parent in a separate residence triggers separate-household allocation.

questions.targetCitation: 26 CFR § 1.2-2(b)(2) (IRC § 2(b) — Head of Household Parent Exception)
questions.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 1.2-2 — Head of Household rules
questions.officialGuideLabel: IRS Publication 501 — Filing Status
questions.goldenQuote: even if the parent does not live in the taxpayer's own home, provided the taxpayer pays more than half the cost of keeping up the parent's separate household for the entire year.
questions.shortestPathHint: 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 1 → § 1.2-2(b)(2) (Special rule for a dependent parent)
socraticHints: This is a classic IRS SEE Part 1 filing status trap testing the residency exception for dependent parents.
Open 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 1 → § 1.2-2 (Head of Household).
Read paragraph (b)(2): unlike other dependents, a dependent parent need NOT live with the taxpayer if the taxpayer pays >50% of maintaining the parent’s separate home all year.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under IRC § 2(b)(1)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.2-2(b)(2), an unmarried taxpayer may claim Head of Household status based on a dependent parent even when the parent lives in a separate residence, provided the taxpayer pays more than half the cost of keeping up the parent’s main home for the entire year and can claim the parent as a dependent.

distractors.A: Incorrect: The same-household residency rule has a statutory exception specifically for a dependent father or mother under IRC § 2(b)(1)(B).
distractors.B: CORRECT: Maya is unmarried, properly claims her mother as a dependent, and pays 70% (>50%) of maintaining her mother’s separate home all year.
distractors.C: Incorrect: Qualifying Surviving Spouse applies only for two tax years after the death of the taxpayer’s own spouse with a dependent child.
distractors.D: Incorrect: No 6-month co-residency is required for a dependent parent living in a separate home funded >50% by the taxpayer.
distractors.E: Incorrect: Married Filing Separately is unavailable to an unmarried taxpayer.

questions.stem:
Daniel provided 75% of the total financial support for his 29-year-old unrelated friend, Owen, whose total gross income for the year was $2,100 (below the qualifying relative gross income limit). Owen is a U.S. citizen, files no joint return, and lived in Daniel’s home from February 1 through December 31 (11 months) before moving in from another city.

Under IRC § 152(d) and 26 CFR § 1.152-1, may Daniel claim Owen as a qualifying relative dependent?

options.text: Yes, because living together for more than half the year (over 6 months) satisfies the residency test for all dependents.
Yes, because Daniel provided more than 50% of Owen’s support and Owen’s gross income was below the statutory limit.
No, because an unrelated individual must live with the taxpayer as a member of the household for the entire taxable year (all 12 months) to satisfy the member-of-household test.
No, because an individual over age 24 can never be claimed as a dependent unless permanently and totally disabled.
Yes, provided Owen signs Form 8332 releasing his personal dependency claim to Daniel.

questions.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 1.152-1 — Definition of a dependent
questions.officialGuideLabel: IRS Publication 501 — Dependents & Filing Information
questions.goldenQuote: A non-relative (such as an unrelated friend) can qualify as a qualifying relative only if the individual lived with the taxpayer as a member of the household for the entire taxable year (all 12 months)
questions.shortestPathHint: 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 1 → § 1.152-1(b) (Qualifying relative tests)
socraticHints: Separate the rules for a Qualifying Child (more than half the year) from an unrelated Qualifying Relative.
Open 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 1 → § 1.152-1(b).
An unrelated friend must live in the taxpayer’s household for the ENTIRE taxable year (January 1 through December 31); 11 months fails the test.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under IRC § 152(d)(2)(H) and 26 CFR § 1.152-1(b), an individual who does not bear a specified family relationship to the taxpayer can be a qualifying relative only if the individual has the same principal place of abode as the taxpayer and is a member of the taxpayer’s household for the ENTIRE taxable year. Living together for 11 months (starting February 1) disqualifies Owen.

distractors.A: Incorrect: The more-than-half-the-year residency test applies to a qualifying child, not an unrelated qualifying relative.
distractors.B: Incorrect: Support and gross income are necessary, but every qualifying relative test (including the full-year household test for non-relatives) must be satisfied.
distractors.C: CORRECT: Non-relatives must be members of the taxpayer’s household for the entire calendar year (all 12 months).
distractors.D: Incorrect: There is no age limit for a qualifying relative; the age 19/24 cap applies only to qualifying children.
distractors.E: Incorrect: Form 8332 is used by a custodial parent to release a child’s dependency claim to a noncustodial parent, not for unrelated friends.

questions.category: IRS SEE Part 1 — Sale of Principal Residence (IRC § 121)
questions.stem:
Elena, a single taxpayer, purchased her home in 2018 for $300,000 and lived in it as her principal residence until selling it in 2025 for $480,000 (net of selling expenses). During ownership, she maintained a qualified home office and properly deducted $18,000 of depreciation after May 6, 1997, reducing her adjusted basis to $282,000 and producing a total realized gain of $198,000.

Under IRC § 121 and 26 CFR § 1.121-1, how much of Elena’s $198,000 gain is excludable and how much must be recognized?

options.text: Exclude all $198,000; recognize $0 because total realized gain is below the $250,000 single exclusion limit.
Exclude $180,000 under IRC § 121; recognize $18,000 of unrecaptured Section 1250 gain attributable to post-May 6, 1997 depreciation.
Exclude $0; recognize all $198,000 because claiming a home office disqualifies the entire home from IRC § 121.
Exclude $180,000; recognize $18,000 as short-term capital gain taxed at 0%.
Exclude $162,000; recognize $36,000 by doubling depreciation recapture for mixed-use residences.

questions.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 1.121-1 — Principal residence gain exclusion
questions.officialGuideLabel: IRS Publication 523 — Selling Your Home
questions.goldenQuote: The Section 121 exclusion does not apply to so much of the gain from the sale of a principal residence as does not exceed the portion of the depreciation adjustments attributable to periods after May 6, 1997
questions.shortestPathHint: 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 1 → § 1.121-1(d) (Depreciation recapture limitation)
socraticHints: Check how post-May 6, 1997 home office depreciation interacts with the $250,000 IRC § 121 exclusion.
Open 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 1 → § 1.121-1(d).
Total gain is $198,000, but the $18,000 depreciation portion cannot be excluded under § 121(d)(6) and is taxed as unrecaptured § 1250 gain; the remaining $180,000 is excluded.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under IRC § 121(d)(6) and 26 CFR § 1.121-1(d), gain attributable to depreciation allowed or allowable after May 6, 1997 cannot be excluded under Section 121. Out of Elena’s $198,000 realized gain, $18,000 must be recognized as unrecaptured Section 1250 gain (max 25% rate), while the remaining $180,000 qualifies for exclusion under her $250,000 single limit.

distractors.A: Incorrect: Post-May 6, 1997 depreciation recapture is carved out of the § 121 exclusion even when total gain is under $250,000.
distractors.B: CORRECT: $18,000 of post-May 6, 1997 depreciation is recognized as unrecaptured § 1250 gain, and $180,000 is excluded.
distractors.C: Incorrect: A home office within the same dwelling unit does not forfeit the § 121 exclusion on the remaining appreciation.
distractors.D: Incorrect: Unrecaptured § 1250 gain is long-term capital gain subject to a maximum 25% rate, not 0% short-term gain.
distractors.E: Incorrect: There is no rule doubling depreciation recapture.

questions.category: IRS SEE Part 1 — Capital Gains & Wash Sales (IRC § 1091)
questions.stem:
On November 10, investor Marcus sold 100 shares of Apex Corp. common stock for $14,000 that he had purchased two years earlier for $20,000 (a $6,000 realized loss). On November 28 (18 days later), Marcus purchased 100 substantially identical shares of Apex Corp. common stock in the same taxable brokerage account for $15,200.

Under IRC § 1091 and 26 CFR § 1.1091-1, what is Marcus’s currently deductible loss and his adjusted tax basis in the replacement 100 shares?

options.text: Deductible loss: $6,000; replacement basis: $15,200.
Deductible loss: $0; replacement basis: $15,200 (the $6,000 loss is permanently lost).
Deductible loss: $0; replacement basis: $21,200 (and the prior holding period tacks onto the replacement shares).
Deductible loss: $3,000 (capital loss limit); replacement basis: $18,200.
Deductible loss: $0; replacement basis: $20,000 (cost of the original shares only).

questions.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 1.1091-1 — Wash sale loss disallowance
questions.officialGuideLabel: IRS Publication 550 — Investment Income and Expenses
questions.goldenQuote: The disallowed wash sale loss is not permanently forfeited in a taxable account; instead, it is added to the basis of the newly acquired replacement stock or securities (IRC § 1091(d))
questions.shortestPathHint: 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 1 → § 1.1091-1 (Losses from wash sales)
socraticHints: Check whether acquiring substantially identical stock 18 days after a loss sale falls within the 30-day before/after wash sale window.
Open 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 1 → § 1.1091-1.
Add the $6,000 disallowed loss to the $15,200 replacement purchase price = $21,200 basis, with tacked holding period.

explanation.correctReasoning: Because Marcus repurchased 100 substantially identical shares within 30 days after the loss sale (18 days later), IRC § 1091 disallows the entire $6,000 loss currently. Under IRC § 1091(d) and 26 CFR § 1.1091-1(f), the $6,000 disallowed loss is added to the $15,200 purchase price of the new shares ($15,200 + $6,000 = $21,200 adjusted basis), and the original 2-year holding period tacks onto the replacement shares.

distractors.A: Incorrect: Reacquiring substantially identical stock within 30 days triggers the wash sale disallowance.
distractors.B: Incorrect: In a taxable brokerage account, the disallowed wash sale loss is deferred into replacement basis, not permanently forfeited (unlike an IRA wash sale under Rev. Rul. 2008-5).
distractors.C: CORRECT: $0 current loss, $21,200 replacement basis ($15,200 + $6,000), and tacked holding period.
distractors.D: Incorrect: The $3,000 net capital loss deduction applies only to allowed losses, not disallowed wash sales.
distractors.E: Incorrect: Replacement basis equals new cost ($15,200) plus disallowed loss ($6,000) = $21,200, not the original $20,000 cost.

questions.stem:
For tax year 2025, Priya is a high-income single taxpayer whose taxable income before the Section 199A deduction is well above the upper phase-in ceiling for IRC § 199A. She operates two separate domestic Schedule C businesses, each paying $0 in W-2 wages and owning $0 in depreciable property (UBIA): (1) an accounting & tax consulting practice (an SSTB), and (2) an independent structural engineering firm.

Under IRC § 199A and 26 CFR § 1.199A-1, which statement accurately describes her QBI deduction eligibility above the upper phase-in ceiling?

options.text: Both businesses are fully excluded as Specified Service Trades or Businesses (SSTBs).
The accounting practice is completely excluded as an SSTB, and although engineering is excluded from the SSTB list, its QBI deduction is still limited to $0 because it has $0 W-2 wages and $0 UBIA.
The engineering firm receives the full 20% QBI deduction because engineering is exempt from both SSTB rules and the W-2 wage/UBIA limits.
Both businesses qualify for a 10% reduced QBI deduction above the phase-in ceiling.
Priya can elect to treat her W-2 salary from an unrelated C corporation employer as QBI to satisfy the wage limitation.

questions.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 1.199A-1 — QBI deduction operational rules
questions.officialGuideLabel: IRS Publication 17 — Your Federal Income Tax
questions.goldenQuote: QBI from an SSTB (such as law, accounting, consulting, health, or financial services — excluding engineering and architecture) is completely disallowed, while non-SSTB businesses are capped by the greater of 50% of W-2 wages or 25% of W-2 wages plus 2.5% of UBIA of qualified property.
questions.shortestPathHint: 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 1 → § 1.199A-1(d) (Threshold and SSTB phase-out)
socraticHints: Check two separate rules above the § 199A phase-in range: (1) which professions are SSTBs vs. statutorily carved out (engineering & architecture), and (2) the W-2 wage / UBIA cap on non-SSTBs.
Open 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 1 → § 1.199A-1(d).
Accounting is an SSTB ($0 above ceiling); engineering is NOT an SSTB, but above the ceiling it is still capped at max(50% W-2 wages, 25% W-2 + 2.5% UBIA) = $0.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under IRC § 199A and 26 CFR § 1.199A-1(d), above the upper phase-in ceiling: (1) an accounting/consulting practice is an SSTB and receives $0 QBI deduction; (2) engineering and architecture are statutorily excluded from SSTB status, BUT a non-SSTB above the ceiling is still capped at the greater of 50% of W-2 wages or 25% of W-2 wages plus 2.5% of UBIA. With $0 W-2 wages and $0 UBIA, the engineering firm’s cap is also $0.

distractors.A: Incorrect: Engineering and architecture are expressly excluded from the statutory SSTB definition under IRC § 199A(d)(2)(A).
distractors.B: CORRECT: Accounting fails as an SSTB, and engineering (a non-SSTB) hits a $0 ceiling due to $0 W-2 wages and $0 UBIA.
distractors.C: Incorrect: Non-SSTBs above the upper threshold are still subject to the W-2 wage / UBIA limitation.
distractors.D: Incorrect: There is no flat 10% reduced QBI rate above the phase-in range.
distractors.E: Incorrect: Employee W-2 wages from an unrelated employer are never QBI and cannot be attributed to a Schedule C business.

questions.category: IRS SEE Part 1 — Gift Tax Exclusions (IRC § 2503)
questions.stem:
During the calendar year, grandmother Evelyn makes three separate transfers for her grandson Leo: (1) she wires $38,000 directly to Leo’s university solely for his undergraduate tuition; (2) she writes a $12,000 check directly to Leo so he can pay his off-campus apartment rent and textbooks; and (3) she transfers $5,000 into an irrevocable trust with NO present withdrawal (Crummey) rights and no income distributions until Leo turns age 35.

Under IRC § 2503 and 26 CFR § 25.2503-2, which transfer(s) require Evelyn to file Form 709 (United States Gift Tax Return)?

options.text: Only the $38,000 university tuition wire, because it exceeds the annual gift tax exclusion.
Only the $5,000 irrevocable trust transfer, because a gift of a future interest never qualifies for the annual exclusion and always requires Form 709.
Both the $38,000 tuition wire and the $12,000 check, because combined transfers to Leo exceed $18,000.
None of the transfers require Form 709 because Evelyn’s total transfers are well below the lifetime unified credit.
Only the $12,000 check for rent and textbooks, because cash gifts to grandchildren are never eligible for the annual exclusion.

questions.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 25.2503-2 — Exclusions from gifts
questions.officialGuideLabel: IRS.gov — Gift Tax FAQs
questions.goldenQuote: A gift of a future interest does not qualify for the annual exclusion and always requires filing Form 709 regardless of dollar amount.
questions.shortestPathHint: 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 1 → § 25.2503-2 (Present interest & direct tuition rules)
socraticHints: Evaluate each of the three transfers separately: direct tuition (IRC § 2503(e)), present-interest cash below the annual exclusion, and a future-interest trust.
Open 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 1 → § 25.2503-2.
Direct tuition to a university is unlimitedly excluded; the $12,000 check is a present interest below the annual exclusion; the $5,000 trust is a future interest requiring Form 709.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under IRC § 2503(e), the $38,000 paid directly to the university for tuition is completely excluded without using any annual exclusion. The $12,000 check to Leo is a present-interest gift well below the annual exclusion. However, the $5,000 transfer to an irrevocable trust with no present withdrawal or current income right is a gift of a future interest under 26 CFR § 25.2503-2(a), which gets $0 annual exclusion and mandates filing Form 709 regardless of amount.

distractors.A: Incorrect: Direct tuition payments to an educational institution are 100% excluded under IRC § 2503(e) and do not require Form 709.
distractors.B: CORRECT: Only the $5,000 future-interest trust transfer fails the annual exclusion and triggers mandatory Form 709 filing.
distractors.C: Incorrect: Direct tuition is excluded under § 2503(e) and does not count toward the annual exclusion threshold.
distractors.D: Incorrect: Future-interest gifts always require filing Form 709 even if $0 gift tax is due because of the lifetime exemption.
distractors.E: Incorrect: Direct cash gifts are classic present-interest gifts eligible for the annual exclusion.

questions.category: IRS SEE Part 2 — S Corporation Stock Basis (IRC § 1367)
questions.stem:
At the beginning of the year, Clara owns 100% of an S corporation (with no C corporation earnings and profits) and has an adjusted stock basis of $20,000 and $0 debt basis. During the year, the S corporation reports: (1) $10,000 of tax-exempt municipal bond interest, (2) a $25,000 cash distribution to Clara, (3) $2,000 of nondeductible fines, and (4) a $15,000 ordinary business loss.

Applying the mandatory IRC § 1367 stock basis ordering rules (26 CFR § 1.1367-1(f)), how much of the $25,000 distribution is taxable capital gain and how much of the $15,000 ordinary loss can Clara deduct this year?

options.text: Taxable distribution gain: $0; deductible ordinary loss: $3,000 (with $12,000 suspended).
Taxable distribution gain: $5,000; deductible ordinary loss: $0 (with $15,000 suspended).
Taxable distribution gain: $12,000; deductible ordinary loss: $15,000.
Taxable distribution gain: $0; deductible ordinary loss: $5,000 (nondeductible fines are ignored until liquidation).
Taxable distribution gain: $0; deductible ordinary loss: $15,000 (stock basis becomes negative -$12,000).

questions.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 1.1367-1 — S corporation stock basis ordering
questions.officialGuideLabel: IRS.gov — S Corporations Stock & Debt Basis
questions.goldenQuote: Because distributions reduce stock basis BEFORE deductible losses, a shareholder may receive tax-free distributions while having excess ordinary losses suspended and carried forward indefinitely
questions.shortestPathHint: 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 2 → § 1.1367-1(f) (4-step basis ordering)
socraticHints: Walk through the exact 4-step S corporation stock basis order: (1) income including tax-exempt, (2) distributions, (3) nondeductible expenses, (4) deductible losses.
Open 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 2 → § 1.1367-1(f).

Compute step by step: $20,000 + $10,000 tax-exempt = $30,000; minus $25,000 distribution = $5,000 ($0 gain); minus $2,000 fines = $3,000; remaining $3,000 allows $3,000 loss deduction ($12,000 suspended).

explanation.correctReasoning: Under IRC § 1367 and 26 CFR § 1.1367-1(f), stock basis is adjusted in strict order: Start $20,000 + Step 1 ($10,000 tax-exempt income) = $30,000. Step 2: Subtract $25,000 distribution -> $5,000 basis remaining ($0 taxable gain). Step 3: Subtract $2,000 nondeductible fines -> $3,000 basis remaining. Step 4: Deduct ordinary loss up to remaining $3,000 basis -> $3,000 deducted currently, ending stock basis $0, and $12,000 suspended loss carried forward indefinitely.

distractors.A: CORRECT: $20k + $10k - $25k = $5k ($0 gain), minus $2k fines = $3k basis left for deductible loss ($12k suspended).
distractors.B: Incorrect: Tax-exempt income DOES increase S corporation stock basis in Step 1, preventing gain on the $25,000 distribution.
distractors.C: Incorrect: Deductible losses cannot be taken before distributions; distributions reduce basis in Step 2 before losses in Step 4.
distractors.D: Incorrect: Nondeductible expenses reduce stock basis in Step 3 before deductible losses in Step 4 (unless an explicit § 1.1367-1(g) election is made).
distractors.E: Incorrect: Stock basis can never be reduced below zero.

questions.category: IRS SEE Part 2 — Partnership Liabilities & Basis (IRC § 752)
questions.stem:
Jordan becomes a 25% limited partner in Harborview LP by contributing $40,000 in cash. Jordan has no obligation to restore a negative capital account and signs no personal loan guarantees. Immediately after formation, Harborview LP borrows: (1) a $100,000 recourse bank line of credit (for which the general partner bears 100% of the economic risk of loss), and (2) a $200,000 qualified nonrecourse real estate mortgage allocated by profit-sharing ratios.

Under IRC § 752 and 26 CFR § 1.752-1, what is Jordan’s adjusted outside basis in Harborview LP?

options.text: $40,000, because limited partners can never include any partnership debt in outside basis.
$65,000 ($40,000 cash plus 25% of the $100,000 recourse bank line only).
$90,000 ($40,000 cash plus 25% of the $200,000 nonrecourse mortgage; $0 of the recourse debt).
$115,000 ($40,000 cash plus 25% of both the $100,000 recourse debt and $200,000 nonrecourse debt).
$240,000 ($40,000 cash plus 100% of the $200,000 nonrecourse mortgage).

questions.targetCitation: 26 CFR § 1.752-1(a)(1)–(2) (IRC § 752 — Partnership Recourse vs. Nonrecourse Debt)
questions.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 1.752-1 — Partnership liabilities
questions.officialGuideLabel: IRS Publication 541 — Partnerships
questions.goldenQuote: nonrecourse liabilities are generally shared by both general and limited partners in accordance with their profit-sharing ratios, allowing limited partners to include a share of nonrecourse debt in outside basis.
questions.shortestPathHint: 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 2 → § 1.752-1(a) (Recourse vs. nonrecourse liabilities)
socraticHints: Distinguish recourse liabilities (allocated to partners bearing economic risk of loss) from nonrecourse liabilities (shared by profit ratios including limited partners).
Open 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 2 → § 1.752-1(a).
Jordan gets $0 of the recourse bank debt (GP bears risk) and 25% × $200,000 = $50,000 of the nonrecourse mortgage -> $40,000 + $50,000 = $90,000.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under IRC § 752 and 26 CFR § 1.752-1(a), recourse liabilities are allocated exclusively to partners who bear the economic risk of loss (here, the general partner receives 100% of the $100,000 recourse line, so limited partner Jordan gets $0). Nonrecourse liabilities are allocated to both general and limited partners by profit-sharing ratios: Jordan’s 25% × $200,000 = $50,000. Total outside basis = $40,000 cash + $50,000 nonrecourse share = $90,000.

distractors.A: Incorrect: Unlike S corporation shareholders (who get zero basis from entity-level third-party debt), limited partners DO receive outside basis for their share of partnership nonrecourse liabilities.
distractors.B: Incorrect: This reverses the recourse vs. nonrecourse rule; Jordan bears zero economic risk of loss on the recourse loan.
distractors.C: CORRECT: $40,000 cash + $0 recourse + $50,000 (25% of $200,000 nonrecourse) = $90,000.
distractors.D: Incorrect: Jordan cannot include 25% of the recourse bank loan without a guarantee or deficit restoration obligation.
distractors.E: Incorrect: Jordan only receives his 25% profit-sharing portion ($50,000), not 100% of the mortgage.

questions.stem:
Sole proprietor Hannah places $85,000 of qualifying 5-year machinery in service during the year and elects Section 179 expensing for the entire $85,000 (well below the statutory dollar cap and phase-out threshold). Before taking the Section 179 deduction, Hannah’s Schedule C net business profit is $52,000, and she also earns $18,000 in W-2 wages from a part-time job.

Under IRC § 179(b)(3) and 26 CFR § 1.179-1(b), what is Hannah’s maximum current-year Section 179 deduction, and what happens to any disallowed excess?

options.text: Deduct $85,000 currently, creating a $33,000 Schedule C net operating loss.
Deduct $52,000 currently (Schedule C profit only); the $33,000 excess is permanently lost.
Deduct $70,000 currently ($52,000 Schedule C profit plus $18,000 W-2 wages); the remaining $15,000 carries forward indefinitely to future tax years.
Deduct $52,000 currently; the remaining $33,000 carries back 2 years and forward 20 years.
Deduct $70,000 currently; the remaining $15,000 must be depreciated immediately using MACRS in the current year instead of carrying forward.

questions.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 1.179-1 — Section 179 expensing rules
questions.officialGuideLabel: IRS Publication 946 — How To Depreciate Property
questions.goldenQuote: aggregate taxable income derived from the active conduct of any trade or business during the taxable year (including W-2 wages for an individual taxpayer, computed without regard to the Section 179 deduction). Any Section 179 amount disallowed solely by the taxable income limitation is carried forward indefinitely
questions.shortestPathHint: 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 2 → § 1.179-1(b) (Taxable income limitation & carryforward)
socraticHints: Remember two critical IRS SEE Part 2 Section 179 rules: (1) W-2 wages count as active trade or business income for individuals, and (2) taxable-income-limited § 179 carries forward indefinitely.
Open 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 2 → § 1.179-1(b).
Aggregate active business taxable income = $52,000 + $18,000 W-2 = $70,000 deductible now; $85,000 - $70,000 = $15,000 carried forward indefinitely.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under IRC § 179(b)(3) and 26 CFR § 1.179-1(b), Section 179 cannot create a net business loss, but for an individual taxpayer, active trade or business taxable income includes W-2 wages ($52,000 Schedule C + $18,000 W-2 = $70,000). The remaining $15,000 elected under Section 179 is disallowed solely by the taxable income limit and carries forward indefinitely to future years.

distractors.A: Incorrect: Unlike MACRS/bonus depreciation, Section 179 cannot exceed aggregate active trade or business taxable income.
distractors.B: Incorrect: W-2 wages ARE included in active business taxable income, and taxable-income-disallowed § 179 is carried forward, not lost.
distractors.C: CORRECT: $70,000 ($52,000 + $18,000) is deductible now and $15,000 carries forward indefinitely.
distractors.D: Incorrect: W-2 wages count toward the income limit, and § 179 carryforwards carry forward indefinitely (no 2-year carryback).
distractors.E: Incorrect: Elected § 179 amounts disallowed by the business income limit carry forward as § 179 carryforward (whereas phase-out reductions from excess asset purchases recover via MACRS).

questions.stem: Which of the following domestic business entities is STRICTLY PROHIBITED from using the cash receipts and disbursements method of accounting under IRC § 448 and 26 CFR § 1.448-2, even if its 3-year average annual gross receipts are only $1,200,000?

options.text: A C corporation retail hardware company with $1,200,000 average annual gross receipts.
A general partnership whose partners include a C corporation, with $1,200,000 average annual gross receipts.
A limited partnership syndicate that allocates 60% of its taxable losses to limited partners (a tax shelter under IRC § 448(d)(3)), with $1,200,000 average annual gross receipts.
An S corporation consulting firm with $1,200,000 average annual gross receipts.
A single-member LLC taxed as a sole proprietorship with $1,200,000 average annual gross receipts.

questions.targetCitation: 26 CFR § 1.448-2(a)–(c) (IRC § 448 — Tax Shelter Cash Method Prohibition)
questions.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 1.448-2 — Limitation on use of the cash method
questions.officialGuideLabel: IRS Publication 538 — Accounting Periods and Methods
questions.goldenQuote: A tax shelter (including a syndicate where more than 35% of losses are allocated to limited partners or limited entrepreneurs) is strictly prohibited from using the cash method regardless of how low its annual gross receipts are.
questions.shortestPathHint: 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 2 → § 1.448-2(c) (Absolute bar for tax shelters)
socraticHints: Check which entity category cannot use the small business gross receipts exception under IRC § 448(c).
Open 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 2 → § 1.448-2.
C corporations and partnerships with C corp partners qualify for cash method under the gross receipts test, whereas tax shelters (including >35% loss syndicates) are strictly barred.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under IRC § 448(a)(3) and 26 CFR § 1.448-2(c), a tax shelter — including a syndicate allocating more than 35% of its losses to limited partners or limited entrepreneurs — is categorically barred from using the cash method regardless of how low its gross receipts are. By contrast, C corporations and partnerships with C corporation partners may use the cash method when they satisfy the IRC § 448(c) small business gross receipts test.

distractors.A: Incorrect: A non-tax-shelter C corporation meeting the § 448(c) gross receipts test may use the cash method.
distractors.B: Incorrect: A partnership with a C corporation partner that meets the § 448(c) gross receipts test may use the cash method.
distractors.C: CORRECT: A tax shelter (syndicate allocating >35% of losses to limited partners) can never use the cash method, regardless of gross receipts.
distractors.D: Incorrect: S corporations are not barred by § 448(a) unless they are tax shelters.
distractors.E: Incorrect: Sole proprietorships are eligible for the cash method unless classified as a tax shelter.

questions.category: IRS SEE Part 2 — Corporate Distributions & E&P (IRC § 301 / § 316)
questions.stem:
Beacon Inc., a C corporation, begins the year with an Accumulated Earnings and Profits (AEP) deficit of ($90,000). During the current year, Beacon Inc. generates positive Current Earnings and Profits (CEP) of $30,000 and distributes $50,000 in cash to its sole shareholder, Victor, whose adjusted stock basis is $12,000.

Under IRC § 301(c), § 316, and 26 CFR § 1.316-2, how must Victor report the $50,000 cash distribution?

options.text: $0 dividend, $12,000 return of capital, and $38,000 capital gain, because combined E&P is negative (-$60,000).
$30,000 taxable dividend, $12,000 nontaxable return of capital, and $8,000 capital gain.
$50,000 taxable dividend because every C corporation cash distribution is a dividend.
$30,000 taxable dividend and $20,000 nontaxable return of capital (stock basis becomes -$8,000).
$12,000 taxable dividend and $38,000 return of capital.

questions.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 1.316-2 — Sources of corporate distributions
questions.officialGuideLabel: IRS Publication 542 — Corporations
questions.goldenQuote: First, as a taxable dividend to the extent of Current Earnings and Profits (CEP), allocated ratably across distributions made during the year — even if the corporation has a large negative Accumulated Earnings and Profits (AEP) deficit
questions.shortestPathHint: 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 2 → § 1.316-2(a) (Current E&P nimble dividend ordering)
socraticHints: Never net positive Current E&P against a negative Accumulated E&P deficit when measuring dividend treatment!
Open 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 2 → § 1.316-2(a).
Allocate the $50,000 distribution in layers: $30,000 CEP = dividend; remaining $20,000 -> first $12,000 reduces stock basis to $0 (return of capital); final $8,000 = capital gain.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under IRC § 316(a)(2) and 26 CFR § 1.316-2(a) (the nimble dividend rule), positive Current E&P ($30,000) is NOT offset by a negative Accumulated E&P deficit (-$90,000). Therefore, of the $50,000 cash distribution: (1) $30,000 is a taxable dividend from CEP; (2) the next $12,000 is a nontaxable return of capital reducing Victor’s stock basis from $12,000 to $0; and (3) the remaining $8,000 is capital gain.

distractors.A: Incorrect: Positive CEP is never netted against an AEP deficit before determining dividend income.
distractors.B: CORRECT: $30,000 dividend (CEP) + $12,000 return of capital (basis) + $8,000 capital gain.
distractors.C: Incorrect: Distributions exceeding both CEP and positive AEP are not dividends.
distractors.D: Incorrect: Stock basis cannot drop below zero; amounts exceeding basis ($8,000) are capital gain.
distractors.E: Incorrect: Dividend income is measured by CEP ($30,000), not stock basis ($12,000).

questions.stem:
Pacific Storage LLC exchanges an investment warehouse (adjusted basis $400,000, fair market value $620,000, unencumbered) for another U.S. commercial investment building (fair market value $580,000) PLUS $40,000 in cash boot. The replacement building is properly identified in writing on Day 35 and closed through a qualified intermediary on Day 140.

Under IRC § 1031 and 26 CFR § 1.1031(a)-1, what is Pacific Storage LLC’s realized gain and recognized gain on this exchange?

options.text: Realized gain: $220,000; recognized gain: $0 because both properties are U.S. commercial real estate.
Realized gain: $220,000; recognized gain: $40,000 (the lesser of realized gain or net boot received).
Realized gain: $180,000; recognized gain: $180,000 because receiving cash boot invalidates the entire IRC § 1031 exchange.
Realized gain: $220,000; recognized gain: $220,000 because the replacement closed after Day 90.
Realized gain: $40,000; recognized gain: $40,000.

questions.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 1.1031(a)-1 — Like-kind real property exchanges
questions.officialGuideLabel: IRS.gov — Like-Kind Exchanges Tax Tips
questions.goldenQuote: gain is recognized to the extent of the LESSER of realized gain or the fair market value of net boot received
questions.shortestPathHint: 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 2 → § 1.1031(a)-1(b)–(c) (Deadlines & boot recognition)
socraticHints: First verify both deferred exchange deadlines (45 days to identify, 180 days to close) and that both assets are investment real property.
Open 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 2 → § 1.1031(a)-1.
Amount realized = $580,000 building + $40,000 cash = $620,000; minus $400,000 basis = $220,000 realized gain; recognized gain = lesser of $220,000 or $40,000 boot = $40,000.

explanation.correctReasoning: Both deadlines are met (identified on Day 35 <= 45 days; closed on Day 140 <= 180 days) and both properties are U.S. investment real property. Amount realized is $580,000 FMV building + $40,000 cash = $620,000; realized gain = $620,000 - $400,000 basis = $220,000. Under IRC § 1031(b) and 26 CFR § 1.1031(a)-1(c), recognized gain equals the lesser of realized gain ($220,000) or boot received ($40,000) = $40,000 (leaving $180,000 deferred).

distractors.A: Incorrect: Receiving cash boot triggers gain recognition up to the lesser of realized gain or boot received.
distractors.B: CORRECT: Realized gain is $220,000 and recognized gain is limited to the $40,000 cash boot.
distractors.C: Incorrect: Boot does not disqualify the entire § 1031 exchange; it triggers partial recognition only up to boot received.
distractors.D: Incorrect: The replacement closing deadline is 180 calendar days (or return due date with extensions), not 90 days.
distractors.E: Incorrect: Realized gain includes both property received and cash ($620,000 - $400,000 = $220,000), not just cash.

questions.category: IRS SEE Part 3 — Representation Authority (26 CFR § 601.504)
questions.stem:
Taxpayer Nora executes ONLY Form 8821 (Tax Information Authorization) naming Enrolled Agent Samuel as her appointee for Form 1040 tax year 2024. The IRS subsequently opens an office audit of Nora’s 2024 return.

Under 26 CFR § 601.504 and IRS Form 2848 / Form 8821 rules, which action is Samuel permitted to take using ONLY Form 8821?

options.text: Advocate Nora’s legal position before the IRS Revenue Agent and negotiate an audit settlement.
Inspect and receive Nora’s confidential 2024 IRS tax transcripts and account information, but NOT advocate her position or represent her before the IRS.
Execute Form 872 extending the statute of limitations on assessment for Nora’s 2024 return.
Sign a binding closing agreement (Form 906) on Nora’s behalf because Samuel holds an active Enrolled Agent credential.
File a Tax Court petition as Nora’s legal counsel without separate admission to the U.S. Tax Court.

questions.targetCitation: 26 CFR § 601.504(a)–(b) (Form 2848 Power of Attorney vs. Form 8821)
questions.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 601.504 — Power of attorney requirements
questions.officialGuideLabel: IRS.gov — About Form 8821 (Tax Information Authorization)
questions.goldenQuote: Form 8821 does NOT authorize the appointee to advocate the taxpayer's position, execute waivers, or otherwise represent the taxpayer before the IRS.
questions.shortestPathHint: 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 3 → § 601.504 (Form 2848 vs. Form 8821)
socraticHints: Compare the scope of Form 8821 (information access only) against Form 2848 (Power of Attorney for representation and advocacy).
Open 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 3 → § 601.504.
Even an active Enrolled Agent cannot advocate, negotiate, or sign waivers for a client without a valid Form 2848 on file.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 26 CFR § 601.504, Form 8821 (Tax Information Authorization) allows the appointee strictly to inspect and receive confidential tax information for the listed matters and years. Regardless of Samuel’s active EA license, he cannot represent Nora, advocate her audit position, or sign waivers/closing agreements unless Nora signs Form 2848 (Power of Attorney).

distractors.A: Incorrect: Advocating a taxpayer’s position before the IRS requires Form 2848.
distractors.B: CORRECT: Form 8821 grants information access only; representation and advocacy require Form 2848.
distractors.C: Incorrect: Executing statute extensions (Form 872) requires a Form 2848 Power of Attorney.
distractors.D: Incorrect: Holding an EA card grants eligibility to represent, but Form 2848 is still required for each client engagement.
distractors.E: Incorrect: Neither Form 8821 nor Form 2848 grants authority to practice before the U.S. Tax Court without Tax Court admission.

questions.category: IRS SEE Part 3 — Assessment Statute of Limitations (IRC § 6501)
questions.stem: Owen filed his 2023 calendar-year return on March 11, 2024. Its prescribed filing date was Monday, April 15, 2024. He reported gross income of $120,000 and omitted an undisclosed $40,000 consulting receipt. There was no fraud, extension or suspension. What is the six-year assessment deadline?

options.text: No deadline applies.

questions.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 301.6501(e)-1 — Substantial omission (6-year rule)
questions.officialGuideLabel: IRS Publication 556 — Examination of Returns & Limitations
questions.goldenQuote: If a taxpayer omits from gross income an amount properly includible therein that is in excess of 25 percent of the amount of gross income stated in the return, the tax may be assessed at any time within 6 years after the return was filed.
questions.shortestPathHint: Read IRC §§ 6501(b)(1), (e)(1)(A) and the study section on substantial omissions.
socraticHints: Compute the 25% comparison on the reported gross income.
Read IRC §§ 6501(b)(1), (e)(1)(A) and the study section on substantial omissions.
Add six years to the prescribed filing date.

explanation.correctReasoning: The omitted $40,000 exceeds 25% of $120,000 ($30,000). The early-filed return is deemed filed April 15, 2024. Six years ends Monday, April 15, 2030.

distractors.A: The actual early-filing date does not start this period, and the omission triggers six years.
distractors.B: The substantial omission extends the period beyond three years.
distractors.C: The omitted $40,000 exceeds 25% of $120,000 ($30,000). The early-filed return is deemed filed April 15, 2024. Six years ends Monday, April 15, 2030.
distractors.D: The six years run from the prescribed date in these facts.
distractors.E: A substantial omission here triggers a six-year period, not an unlimited one.

questions.category: IRS SEE Part 3 — Collection Due Process (IRC § 6330)
questions.stem:
On May 1, the IRS sends taxpayer Rebecca a Final Notice of Intent to Levy and Notice of Your Right to a Hearing (Letter 1058 / LT11). Rebecca asks her Enrolled Agent to request a Collection Due Process (CDP) hearing on Form 12153 to propose an installment agreement and preserve her right to petition the U.S. Tax Court if Appeals rules against her.

Under IRC § 6330 and 26 CFR § 301.6330-1, within how many days must Form 12153 be submitted to preserve Tax Court judicial review, and what happens if she files it 60 days later instead?

options.text: Within 90 calendar days; filing after 90 days forfeits all IRS Appeals review.
Within 30 calendar days from the day after the notice date; filing 60 days later qualifies only for an Equivalent Hearing, which does NOT preserve U.S. Tax Court review.
Within 60 calendar days; filing on Day 60 still preserves full U.S. Tax Court appeal rights.
Within 10 business days; filing after 10 days requires full payment of the tax before requesting a refund.
Within 1 year; both CDP hearings and Equivalent Hearings provide identical U.S. Tax Court appeal rights.

questions.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 301.6330-1 — Notice & hearing prior to levy
questions.officialGuideLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 301.6320-1 — CDP Hearing on Federal Tax Lien
questions.goldenQuote: The taxpayer must submit a written request (Form 12153) within 30 calendar days beginning on the day after the date of the Final Notice of Intent to Levy.
questions.shortestPathHint: 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 3 → § 301.6330-1(b) & (e) (30-day CDP vs. Equivalent Hearing)
socraticHints: Do not confuse the 90-day Notice of Deficiency deadline with the 30-day Collection Due Process (CDP) hearing deadline.
Open 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 3 → § 301.6330-1.
Timely Form 12153 must be filed within 30 days to suspend levy and preserve Tax Court review; a late request (within 1 year) yields an Equivalent Hearing with NO Tax Court review.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under IRC § 6330 and 26 CFR § 301.6330-1(b) and (e), Form 12153 must be requested within 30 calendar days after the Final Notice of Intent to Levy to suspend levy action and preserve U.S. Tax Court judicial review. Filing 60 days later (still within 1 year) grants only an administrative Equivalent Hearing, whose Decision Letter cannot be appealed to the U.S. Tax Court.

distractors.A: Incorrect: 90 days is the Statutory Notice of Deficiency (90-day letter) deadline for Tax Court, not the 30-day CDP deadline.
distractors.B: CORRECT: 30 days for CDP with Tax Court rights; after 30 days (up to 1 year) yields only an Equivalent Hearing without Tax Court appeal rights.
distractors.C: Incorrect: Day 60 misses the 30-day CDP window and loses Tax Court judicial review.
distractors.D: Incorrect: The CDP deadline is 30 calendar days, not 10 business days.
distractors.E: Incorrect: Equivalent Hearings do not suspend collection statutes or confer U.S. Tax Court jurisdiction.

questions.category: IRS SEE Part 3 — Preparer Due Diligence (IRC § 6695(g))
questions.stem:
Paid tax preparer Kevin prepares a client’s Form 1040 claiming Head of Household filing status, the Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), the Child Tax Credit (CTC), and the American Opportunity Tax Credit (AOTC). Kevin skips Form 8867 altogether and retains zero supporting documents.

Under IRC § 6695(g) and 26 CFR § 1.6695-2, how many separate due diligence penalties may the IRS assess on this single return, and how long must preparers retain Form 8867 records?

options.text: One single combined penalty per tax return; retain records for 1 year.
Up to four separate IRC § 6695(g) penalties (one each for HOH, EITC, CTC, and AOTC); retain Form 8867 and reliance records for 3 years.
Only one penalty for EITC (Form 8867 does not cover Head of Household or AOTC); retain records for 5 years.
Up to two penalties (one for filing status, one for all credits combined); retain records for 7 years.
Zero penalties if the taxpayer signed Form 8879 e-file authorization.

questions.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 1.6695-2 — Paid preparer due diligence
questions.officialGuideLabel: IRS.gov — About Form 8867 (Due Diligence Checklist)
questions.goldenQuote: Penalties under IRC § 6695(g) are assessed separately for EACH covered benefit on the same return (meaning up to four separate penalties on a single return).
questions.shortestPathHint: 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 3 → § 1.6695-2 (4 covered benefits & 3-year retention)
socraticHints: List all four Form 8867 covered items: EITC, CTC/ACTC/ODC, AOTC, and Head of Household.
Open 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 3 → § 1.6695-2.
IRC § 6695(g) stacks per failure on the same return (up to 4 penalties), and record retention is 3 years.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under IRC § 6695(g) and 26 CFR § 1.6695-2, Form 8867 due diligence applies to four specific tax benefits: EITC, CTC/ACTC/ODC, AOTC, and Head of Household status. Failure to comply triggers a separate statutory penalty for EACH benefit claimed on the same return (up to 4 separate penalties on one Form 1040), and preparers must retain Form 8867, worksheets, and client reliance records for 3 years.

distractors.A: Incorrect: Penalties are assessed per covered benefit failure (up to 4 per return), and retention is 3 years, not 1 year.
distractors.B: CORRECT: Up to 4 separate § 6695(g) penalties on one return, with mandatory 3-year document retention.
distractors.C: Incorrect: Form 8867 covers all four benefits (EITC, CTC/ACTC/ODC, AOTC, and HOH), and retention is 3 years.
distractors.D: Incorrect: Each of the four covered benefits triggers its own separate penalty, and retention is 3 years.
distractors.E: Incorrect: Signing Form 8879 does not relieve the paid preparer of IRC § 6695(g) due diligence duties.

questions.stem:
Individual taxpayer Trevor (who does NOT claim the IRC § 199A QBI deduction) files Form 1040 showing $38,000 of tax. Upon audit, the IRS determines Trevor’s correct tax required to be shown is $44,000, creating a $6,000 understatement attributable to an aggressive, undisclosed deduction lacking substantial authority and lacking reasonable cause.

Under IRC § 6662(d) and 26 CFR § 1.6662-3, does Trevor’s $6,000 understatement constitute a substantial understatement of income tax, and what is the applicable accuracy-related penalty?

options.text: No, because $6,000 is less than 25% of the $44,000 tax required to be shown ($0 penalty).
Yes, because $6,000 exceeds the greater of 10% of the $44,000 tax required to be shown ($4,400) or $5,000; the 20% accuracy-related penalty is $1,200.
Yes, and the penalty stacks to 40% ($2,400) because both negligence and substantial understatement apply to the same $6,000.
No, because individual substantial understatement applies only when the understatement exceeds $10,000.
Yes, and the fraud penalty of 75% ($4,500) applies automatically to any undisclosed position.

questions.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 26 CFR § 1.6662-3 — Accuracy-related penalty rules
questions.officialGuideLabel: IRS.gov — Accuracy-Related Penalty
questions.goldenQuote: For an individual taxpayer, an understatement of income tax is substantial if it exceeds the GREATER of 10 percent of the tax required to be shown on the return or $5,000
questions.shortestPathHint: 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 3 → § 1.6662-3 (20% penalty & greater of 10% or $5,000)
socraticHints: Compare the $6,000 understatement against the GREATER of 10% of $44,000 ($4,400) or $5,000.
Open 26 CFR / IRC (SEE) → SEE Part 3 → § 1.6662-3.
$6,000 > $5,000 -> substantial understatement! Accuracy-related penalty = 20% × $6,000 = $1,200 (and § 6662 components never stack on the same dollars).

explanation.correctReasoning: Under IRC § 6662(d)(1)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.6662-3(b), an individual’s understatement is substantial if it exceeds the GREATER of 10% of the tax required to be shown ($4,400) or $5,000. Here, $6,000 > $5,000, so the 20% accuracy-related penalty applies: 20% × $6,000 = $1,200. Components of § 6662 (negligence and substantial understatement) do not stack on the same underpayment portion.

distractors.A: Incorrect: 25% is the gross income omission threshold for the 6-year statute of limitations (§ 6501(e)), not the § 6662 substantial understatement threshold.
distractors.B: CORRECT: $6,000 exceeds $5,000 (the greater of $4,400 or $5,000), yielding a 20% penalty of $1,200.
distractors.C: Incorrect: Under 26 CFR § 1.6662-2(c), the 20% accuracy-related penalty does not stack to 40% for negligence plus substantial understatement on the same dollars.
distractors.D: Incorrect: $10,000 is the threshold for C corporations, not individuals ($5,000).
distractors.E: Incorrect: The 75% civil fraud penalty (IRC § 6663) requires the IRS to prove fraudulent intent by clear and convincing evidence.

questions.category: IRS SEE Part 3 — EA Renewal, CE & Sanctions (31 CFR § 10.6 & § 10.50)
questions.stem:
Enrolled Agent Lydia is in a full 3-year enrollment renewal cycle. During Year 1 she completes 30 hours of qualifying federal tax continuing education (including 2 hours of ethics). During Year 2 she completes 12 hours of qualifying federal tax CE (including 2 hours of ethics). During Year 3 she completes 32 hours of qualifying federal tax CE (including 2 hours of ethics), totaling 74 hours over the 3-year cycle.

Under 31 CFR § 10.6(e) (Circular 230), has Lydia satisfied the continuing education requirements to renew her active EA status on Form 8554?

options.text: Yes, because her 3-year total of 74 hours exceeds the 72-hour requirement and she completed 6 hours of ethics.
No, because Circular 230 requires a minimum of 16 hours of continuing education (including 2 hours of ethics) in EACH individual year of the 3-year enrollment cycle, and Year 2 had only 12 hours.
No, because Enrolled Agents must complete 40 hours per year (120 hours per 3-year cycle).
Yes, because excess hours from Year 1 (14 excess hours) automatically carry over to cover the Year 2 shortfall.
No, because ethics requires 4 hours per year (12 hours total per 3-year cycle).

questions.officialSourceLabel: eCFR: 31 CFR § 10.6 — Term and renewal of EA status
questions.officialGuideLabel: IRS.gov — Enrolled Agent Renewal & CE
questions.goldenQuote: must be completed during each enrollment year of an enrollment cycle
questions.shortestPathHint: 31 CFR Part 10 → Subparts A & C → § 10.6(e) (72-hour cycle & 16-hour annual minimum)
socraticHints: Check BOTH the 3-year total (72 hours) AND the strict per-year minimum (16 hours including 2 ethics hours each year).
Open 31 CFR Part 10 → Subparts A & C → § 10.6(e).
Even though 30 + 12 + 32 = 74 >= 72, Lydia fell short of the mandatory 16-hour annual minimum in Year 2 (only 12 hours) and excess hours do NOT carry over.

explanation.correctReasoning: Under 31 CFR § 10.6(e), an Enrolled Agent must complete BOTH at least 72 hours over the 3-year enrollment cycle AND a minimum of 16 hours (including 2 hours of ethics) in EACH individual year of the cycle. Completing only 12 hours in Year 2 violates the 16-hour annual minimum, and excess CE hours from Year 1 cannot be carried over to cure Year 2.

distractors.A: Incorrect: Meeting the 72-hour 3-year total does not waive the mandatory 16-hour minimum for each individual year.
distractors.B: CORRECT: Year 2 had only 12 hours, failing the mandatory 16-hour per-year floor under 31 CFR § 10.6(e).
distractors.C: Incorrect: The Circular 230 requirement is 72 hours per 3-year cycle (16 hours/year min), not 120 hours (which is a typical CPA CPE standard).
distractors.D: Incorrect: Circular 230 does not allow excess CE hours from one year to carry forward to satisfy another year’s 16-hour minimum.
distractors.E: Incorrect: Ethics requires 2 hours per year (6 hours per 3-year cycle), not 4 hours per year.
